title: Especie amenazada: rescatan un aguará guazú en Rosario y lo trasladan a un centro de fauna de Santa Fe
content:
Especie amenazada: rescatan un aguará guazú en Rosario y lo trasladan a un centro de fauna de Santa Fe
El animal fue encontrado deambulando en el oeste-sur de Rosario y quedó bajo resguardo de la Policía Ecológica; será trasladado a La Esmeralda, donde será evaluado antes de definir una eventual liberación
- 3 minutos de lectura'
Un aguará guazú fue rescatado este miércoles en el oeste-sur de Rosario, luego de que trabajadores de una empresa ubicada en las inmediaciones de las avenidas Uriburu y Circunvalación alertaran sobre la presencia del animal.
Personal de la Policía Ecológica de Santa Fe intervino en el lugar y logró poner al ejemplar a resguardo. El animal será trasladado al Centro de Rescate, Interpretación e Investigación de la Fauna “La Esmeralda”, en la ciudad de Santa Fe, donde será sometido a una evaluación veterinaria.
El aguará guazú (Chrysocyon brachyurus) es el cánido más grande de Sudamérica y también es conocido como lobo de crin, pero parece en realidad un zorro con patas alargadas como las de una garza.
Su nombre significa literalmente “zorro grande” en guaraní. Es un animal omnívoro que se alimenta de pequeños mamíferos, aves, reptiles, anfibios, insectos y peces, además de frutos silvestres.
El aguará guazú no representa un peligro para las personas. Es un animal solitario y de hábitos principalmente crepusculares y nocturnos.
Con presencia en las provincias de Corrientes, Formosa, Chaco, norte de Santa Fe y Córdoba, el este de Santiago del Estero y el sur de Misiones, el aguará guazú está catalogado a nivel nacional como especie amenazada. Fue declarado Monumento Natural de la provincia de Santa Fe. Por ese motivo, las autoridades activaron el protocolo sanitario y de protección previsto para estos casos, de acuerdo con la Ley Provincial N.º 12.182.
En La Esmeralda, los equipos veterinarios y técnicos realizarán un diagnóstico para determinar el estado de salud del ejemplar. También evaluarán sus condiciones antes de definir una eventual liberación. El regreso a la naturaleza se concretará únicamente si los especialistas consideran que el animal está en condiciones de sobrevivir por sus propios medios.
Otros rescates
El caso de Rosario se suma a otros rescates y posteriores liberaciones de aguará guazú realizados por la provincia. En marzo de este año, un ejemplar que había sido encontrado en la localidad de Soledad, en el departamento San Cristóbal, fue trasladado a La Esmeralda. El animal presentaba bajo peso y una lesión grave en una de sus orejas. Después de completar su rehabilitación y los controles correspondientes, fue liberado en una zona rural.
En junio, otro aguará guazú que había sido encontrado en Monte Vera fue rehabilitado en La Esmeralda y posteriormente liberado. El operativo formó parte de las acciones de rescate y reinserción de fauna silvestre que lleva adelante la provincia.
También en 2025 un ejemplar joven que había sido encontrado dentro de un galpón en Coronda pasó por La Esmeralda antes de ser liberado en la Reserva Natural El Fisco. En ese caso, el animal fue equipado con un collar de telemetría para permitir el seguimiento de sus desplazamientos.

title: YODAS v3: Over 1 Million Hours of High-Bandwidth, Stereophonic, Multilingual Speech
content: We present YODAS v3, a weakly-labeled speech corpus containing over 1.1 million hours of 48kHz multi-channel audio in 147 languages, released under a CC BY 3.0 license. YODAS v3 is not only the largest open speech dataset to date, but also the first truly large-scale speech corpus with high-fidelity stereo audio. We first provide the collection methodology for the corpus, where we introduce new techniques for gathering language-balanced speech data. The effectiveness of our approach is shown by the language distribution of the crawled data: 22 languages in YODAS v3 have over 10K hours and 73 languages have over 5K hours of data. We then conduct extensive analyses on the composition of the data, such as the distribution of languages, audio quality, and transcription quality. Finally, we train baseline speech recognition and neural codec models to show the effectiveness of the dataset. Download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/espnet/yodas3.

title: Atacama : un "désert fleuri" exceptionnel et resplendissant après les pluies d'El Niño
content:
Des pluies exceptionnelles provoquées par El Niño dans le nord du Chili ont transformé le désert d'Atacama en un vaste tapis de fleurs, ce qui pourrait constituer l'un des épisodes de "désert fleuri" les plus importants jamais observés.
Sous le sol de ce désert, l'un des plus arides du globe, se cachent les graines et bulbes d'environ 200 espèces, qui attendent les précipitations pour germer. Parmi ces espèces, des suspiros blancos et des patas de guanaco, qui teintent de violet de vastes étendues.
Les touristes arrêtent leurs véhicules au bord de la route pour prendre des photos de ce paysage transformé, qui peut inclure un arc-en-ciel mêlé au rouge intense du coucher du soleil.
Le désert fleuri, qui s'étend entre dunes et plaines, est "plus que des fleurs", note auprès de l'AFP César Pizarro, chef de la section de conservation de la biodiversité de la Corporation nationale forestière chilienne (Conaf) dans l'Atacama.
Les abeilles pollinisent les plantes, tandis que les coléoptères se nourrissent de leurs restes et enrichissent le sol de leurs excréments, riches en azote et en phosphore, explique-t-il.
"Bien qu'il existe plusieurs déserts qui fleurissent lorsqu'il pleut, l'ampleur territoriale et la diversité d'espèces qui existent ici sont uniques", note M. Pizarro.
Les pluies de cet hiver austral ont dépassé les 180 millimètres en certains points de la région, "des niveaux très élevés qui n'avaient jamais été enregistrés" auparavant, explique l'expert. L'eau a pénétré plus profondément dans le sable et a activé davantage de vie.
Selon la Conaf, le désert fleuri, comme on appelle cet événement naturel, atteindra cette année son apogée en octobre, sur environ 15.000 hectares.
"Le phénomène El Niño cette année, bien qu'il suscite une grande préoccupation (...) en raison des impacts qu'il provoque dans de nombreux endroits, génère aussi de la vie ou active la vie", souligne M. Pizarro.
Une forte évaporation de l'eau dans le Pacifique, au large du Pérou, a provoqué des pluies torrentielles dans le nord du Chili entre le 16 et le 22 juillet, rappelle-t-il.
Ces pluies ont fait 13 morts et détruit ou gravement endommagé environ 4.000 logements, selon les autorités.
Lire aussiL'écosystème unique du désert d'Atacama menacé par les déchets du monde
El Niño, une variation naturelle du climat qui se produit tous les deux à sept ans, élève les températures de surface au centre et à l'est du Pacifique équatorial, ce qui entraîne des changements mondiaux dans les vents et les précipitations, ainsi que des conditions météorologiques erratiques.
"Pour notre pays, le désert fleuri est une fierté, il fait partie de notre patrimoine", déclare César Pizarro au milieu de pousses jaunes se dressant dans le sable.

title: Ready
content:
For almost seven years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to move forward with grief.
I’ve been walking into rooms with it. Bringing it to work with me. Walking down the grocery aisle with it. Sitting on the couch with it. I have even brought grief with me on dates, which went as awkwardly as you are imagining.
I’ve been donning its weight like a cloak. Like an identity because somehow that felt like I was honoring his life – proving how much I love and miss him. Assuring myself with every second, that I am not forgetting my husband.
I have dutifully and relentlessly cried myself to sleep. I have refused to make friends. Refused to build professional community at work. Refused to be part of my church community. I told myself I could no longer participate in things that produce joy, happiness, or any sense of belonging. A widow mourns the love of her life; she does not go about enjoying things.
I have done everything worthy of suffering the greatest loss of my life, but none of it – not a single act – has brought me any healing. Rather, it has only ensured deep, painful loneliness and an isolation I never thought imaginable.
I do not know why grievers do this, but I know I am not the first. I do not know how long it was supposed to take to realize that this is not the way JD would have wanted me to honor his life, only that it took me almost seven years. Perhaps for others it took less time. For some, it may take longer. Perhaps there are even those who will grieve this way forever. For each of us, the pilgrimage of grief winds differently.
What I do know, finally, is this:
I know what it feels like to be ready for something different.
What it feels like to remove the cloak of grief without forgetting it.
What it feels like to be ready to live again.
I am ready.
I am ready to heal and mature in Christ so much that He’s able to use me and my testimony to help others.
I am ready to have so many friendships that it doesn’t seem real or possible to have this many friends. I am ready for community at work, with my church, and with my family.
I am ready.
I am done feeling jaded, and cynical, and negative, and resentful, and forsaken.
I am ready to embrace good things. I am ready to smile about the wonderful life I had the blessing of experiencing with my husband as we raised our children and navigated life together.
I am ready to make new memories.
I am ready to move forward in a different way. Not as a woman whose identity rests in the title of widow, but as a woman who loves God, loves people, and helps others access joy, even when joy feels impossible to regain.
I am ready.

title: Unas vacas olvidadas en una isla sobrevivieron solas durante 130 años y su extraordinaria adaptación fascina a los científicos
content: Aislamiento bovino - La población alcanzó unos 2.000 ejemplares pese al aislamiento, acumuló cerca del 30% de consanguinidad y pudo reducir los efectos del cuello de botella fundacional Las vacas de la isla de Ámsterdam acabaron pagando un precio bastante alto por haberse convertido en unas supervivientes extraordinarias, ya que su presencia amenazaba a especies autóctonas de este remoto territorio francés. La situación llevó a construir una valla en 1987 y retirar 1.059 animales del sector meridional entre 1988 y 1989. La preocupación afectaba especialmente al albatros de Ámsterdam y al árbol Phylica arborea. Finalmente, en 2010 fueron sacrificados los últimos ejemplares de vacas como parte de un programa de restauración ecológica. La recuperación de la vegetación continuó posteriormente con plantaciones de árboles autóctonos, y en 2019 la UNESCO incorporó las Tierras y Mares Australes Franceses a su Lista del Patrimonio Mundial. La genética revela dos procedencias entre aquellas vacas La extinción de aquella población impidió volver a estudiar animales vivos, pero varias muestras biológicas obtenidas años antes conservaron información sobre sus orígenes. Gracias a ese material, una investigación publicada en julio de 2024 en la revista Molecular Biology and Evolution ha permitido reconstruir parte de su historia genética. El estudio, encabezado por Mathieu Gautier, investigador en genómica de poblaciones y evolución del INRAE, identificó dos grandes componentes genéticos. Aproximadamente el 75% procedía de ganado taurino europeo relacionado con la actual raza Jersey, mientras que el 25% restante correspondía a cebúes del océano Índico vinculados con poblaciones de Madagascar y Mayotte. Los investigadores plantean que esta diversidad pudo existir ya antes de la llegada de los animales y favorecer su supervivencia. La posibilidad de reconstruir la historia genética de una población extinguida dependió de unas muestras biológicas que habían permanecido conservadas desde dos expediciones científicas anteriores. Los investigadores recuperaron ADN de 18 animales examinados en 1992 y 2006 y realizaron la secuenciación del genoma completo de ocho ejemplares. Posteriormente, compararon los resultados con numerosas poblaciones bovinas de distintas regiones del mundo. La conservación de esas muestras resultó especialmente importante porque la eliminación definitiva del ganado se había realizado sin un programa coordinado para preservar su patrimonio biológico. Aquellos restos permitieron estudiar una historia evolutiva que ya había terminado. Cinco reses iniciaron una población independiente durante un siglo La isla de Ámsterdam se encuentra en el sur del océano Índico, a unos 4.400 kilómetros al sureste de Madagascar, y ocupa aproximadamente 54 kilómetros cuadrados. Su clima oceánico está caracterizado por temperaturas frescas, precipitaciones frecuentes y vientos capaces de alcanzar fuerza huracanada. La ausencia de fuentes permanentes de agua dulce añade otra dificultad para los grandes mamíferos terrestres. La presencia humana también ha sido reducida, con una base científica establecida en 1949. Las condiciones ambientales hacían especialmente interesante averiguar cómo había logrado establecerse allí una población de ganado doméstico sin cuidados humanos. Ninguna de aquellas reses existe ya El origen de aquella población se remonta a 1871, cuando un agricultor llamado Heurtin llegó desde la isla de Reunión con cinco reses para intentar establecerse en Ámsterdam. El proyecto de colonización fracasó al cabo de unos meses y el hombre abandonó el territorio, pero dejó atrás a los animales. A partir de entonces comenzó un proceso de asilvestramiento por el que sus descendientes aprendieron a vivir y reproducirse sin intervención humana. La población terminó convirtiéndose en uno de los casos mejor documentados de ganado doméstico que recuperó una existencia independiente durante más de un siglo. Los genes cuestionan el supuesto enanismo de aquellas reses abandonadas a su suerte El tamaño corporal de aquellas vacas también provocó una polémica científica que enfrentó distintas interpretaciones sobre su evolución en condiciones de aislamiento geográfico. En 2017, Roberto Rozzi y Mark V. Lomolino publicaron en Scientific Reports una investigación que atribuía al enanismo insular una reducción del tamaño de los animales hasta aproximadamente tres cuartas partes del original. El análisis genético posterior cuestionó esa explicación al plantear que los fundadores ya pertenecían a variedades bovinas pequeñas. Tampoco encontró pruebas genéticas concluyentes de una selección encaminada a reducir su tamaño. En cambio, identificó posibles señales de selección en genes relacionados con el sistema nervioso, compatibles con cambios de comportamiento. La expansión de la población permitió que aquel pequeño grupo fundador de pequeño tamaño alcanzara unos 2.000 ejemplares en 1952, una cifra que volvió a registrarse aproximadamente en 1988. Los estudios demográficos también identificaron una reproducción estacional, con alrededor del 80% de los nacimientos concentrados en cuatro meses. Pese al crecimiento y a la recuperación tras episodios de enfermedad y reducción poblacional, el aislamiento tuvo consecuencias genéticas. Los investigadores calcularon una consanguinidad individual cercana al 30%, una situación que aumenta el riesgo de enfermedades hereditarias. Sin embargo, tampoco encontraron pruebas concluyentes de una eliminación sistemática de mutaciones perjudiciales mediante selección natural. Su hipótesis apunta a que la rápida expansión acortó los efectos del cuello de botella inicial y ayudó a conservar parte de la diversidad de una población fundada por apenas cinco animales.

title: Operationalization of the African Medicines Agency: Retrospective evaluation of the continental centralized pilot procedure timelines to recommendation and national registrations.
content: Regulatory inconsistency across Africa causes duplicative assessments, prolonged approvals, and delayed medical access. To inform the African Medicines Agency (AMA), the African Medicines Regulatory Harmonisation (AMRH) piloted Africa's first continental scientific evaluation of human medicinal products. This study evaluates the pilot's performance and how scientific opinions translated into national decisions. A mixed-methods evaluation used regulatory datasets from the pilot. Data included assessment timelines, GMP inspections, and national actions. Thematic analysis identified uptake determinants. Of 64 expressions of interest, 24 progressed to evaluation, and 12 received positive opinions. Ten met the ≤210-day target. Twenty-four GMP inspections found deficiencies aligned with global standards. National uptake: full reliance for 7 products (58%); sequential reliance for 3 (25%); separate assessment for 2 (17%). Some products registered in up to 23 countries within a median of 77 working days post-recommendation. Uptake variability reflected legal authority, administrative requirements and submission strategies. The pilot shows a continent-wide regulatory mechanism is feasible and can produce trusted scientific outputs and enable reliance-based national decisions in Africa. Despite widespread reliance, heterogeneity in procedures and sequencing affected registration time. These findings provide empirical evidence for AMA scale-up, emphasizing the need for harmonised pathways, streamlined administration and digital infrastructure.

title: Executive summary of the Integrated Clinical care pathway for the detection and management of preclinical stages of type 1 diabetes: SED-SEEN-SEEP consensus.
content: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) can be identified in preclinical stages through the detection of islet autoantibodies and staged before clinical onset. This evolving paradigm highlights the need for structured care models allowing coordinated identification, staging, and follow-up of individuals with positive islet autoimmunity. This document describes an Integrated Care Pathway (ICP) developed from the available scientific evidence and the national SED-SEEN-SEEP consensus on screening and monitoring of preclinical T1D. The model is organised into three core sub-processes (target population identification, autoantibody detection and confirmation, and clinical follow-up with staging) and one transversal support sub-process based on information systems and performance indicators. This ICP provides a structured, evaluable, and scalable framework for the homogeneous implementation of screening and follow-up of preclinical T1D.

title: 'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
content:
'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
- Published
Wearing a special jersey on the day of the big game, sitting in the exact same seat match after match, or maybe donning some lucky underpants.
These are just some of the rituals sports fans believe can help their team win.
But 10-year-old Eoghan decided it was time to step up his fan game.
For him, the best chance to ensure success would be to wear his Tyrone GAA colours while meeting Pope Leo XIV.
"I was wearing the jersey because I thought it would make Tyrone special."
Eoghan, along with his older sister Áine and mum Edel Quinn, met the Pope in August after a friend arranged tickets to one of his weekly public audiences.
Áine says they did not realise how close they were going to be to the pontiff until they arrived at St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City.
"They led us up to the very front, we were gobsmacked."
The Castlederg family were even more surprised when they found out they would have a chance to chat with Pope Leo.
Eoghan says he shook his hand first, then Áine's and then their mum's.
"He was looking at the jersey wondering where it was from."
Áine says the Pope then acknowledged how far they had travelled.
Eoghan thinks the Pope may have recognised the jersey, as this was not the first time he came into contact with one.
In November 2025, Aidan Gallagher tossed a Tyrone jersey with 'Leo 14' written on the back of it to the pontiff outside the Vatican.
And the Tyrone connection did not stop once the meeting was over.
After receiving a blessing from the Pope and rosary beads from one of the guards, Áine says they were escorted down an aisle where hundreds of people were watching them from behind barricades.
From out of nowhere, someone in the crowd shouted "up Tyrone!".
"I could not believe it walking down seeing all those different faces and then someone says up Tyrone."
Besides the excitement of meeting the Pope, it was also an emotional day for the siblings, as Edel has Multiple Sclerosis
"Our faith is important to us, we always went to mass every Saturday or Sunday and my mum has MS, so the trip was very special for her," says Áine.
The family still cannot not believe it really happened.
Eoghan says his friends have all been asking him: "How do you shake hands with the Pope?"
While Áine says people have grabbing the hand the pontiff shook: "Being just two ordinary people from Castlederg, sitting inches from the Pope and meeting him, it was surreal."

title: Australian finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize 'nervous but excited'
content:
Indigenous rangers among finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize
In short:
An alliance of 70 Indigenous ranger groups who use traditional knowledge to manage Australia's bushfire risks are finalists in Prince William's Earthshot Prize.
They have been recognised for their work to reduce fuel loads and restore biodiversity across the Australian desert.
What's next?
Winners in five categories will be announced in Mumbai on November 17, each taking away a prize worth $1.9 million.
Indigenous rangers responsible for one of the largest cultural burning programs in the world have been named finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize.
The prize, which comes with $1.9 million to support each winner's work, aims to reward environmental projects "that will drive significant progress towards repairing the planet".
Samantha Murray, CEO of the Indigenous Desert Alliance (IDA), said she was proud the network of 70 ranger teams across Central Australia had been given global recognition.
"To be recognised on such a massive scale is something that we work really hard at, to make sure that desert rangers are known, they're heard, they're seen."
More than 150 judges selected the IDA from among 7,000 nominations from 169 countries, with Ms Murray admitting she was "slightly nervous, but really excited" about the alliance's prospects.
In the past four years the alliance has engaged 1,300 Indigenous participants, trained 885 rangers and managed fuel loads and restored biodiversity across 145 million hectares of land — an area four times the size of Germany.
Ms Murray, a proud Yilka, Wongutha and Nyoongar woman, said the Right Way Fire program, which combines cultural and Western ways of burning, was key to their nomination for the prize.
The rangers conduct targeted burns to create a mosaic of vegetation which reduces fuel loads, improves native habitats and lessens the risk of large, destructive bushfires.
"Those ways of reading country are when to burn, who to burn by the right people, what times, what weather, what country," Ms Murray said.
She said alliance, formed more than a decade ago, relied on land management practices developed and passed down over tens of thousands of years.
"It really just helped to elevate the way my desert people have been connecting for a very, very long time across different country," she said.
"It's really big about making sure we're continuing that caring for country from our ancestors and our elders, for ourselves and our children."
Prince impressed by 'scale' of IDA's work: CEO
Prince William created the Earthshot Prize in 2020, saying he wanted to reward new ideas and technologies for tackling climate change.
Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said the prince would be among those who decided who would win in Mumbai in November.
"I think he was absolutely amazed by just the scale [of IDA's work]," he said.
"To have one initiative that is protecting 2.7 million square kilometres — we haven't seen anything like that in the previous six years."
The IDA is one of three finalists in Earthshot's "protect and restore nature" category.
It is up against the Himalayan country Bhutan, which has enshrined environmental protection in its constitution, and the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative which protects habitats along the Rocky Mountains on the Canada-US border.
Mr Knauf said investing in the knowledge of Indigenous people was key to meeting the global commitment of protecting and conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030.
"Indigenous communities right around the world who are protecting a disproportionate share of the land that we all rely on for our economy … have the deep knowledge about what is going to work in the face of climate change."
If the IDA won, Ms Murray said the funds would boost the alliance's fire protection work, as well as increase the grants available for projects such as trips on country for intergenerational knowledge transfer or ranger exchanges.
She would like to see more desert communities having a "visible presence" in global conversations about climate change.
"We can't ignore the impacts of climate change and how it's impacting and shaping country a little bit differently and making it much harder for desert rangers out there," she said.
'Loudest voice in any room'
Australia has been a strong contender for the prize in the past, with the Indigenous Women Rangers Network in Queensland winning the "revive our oceans" category in 2022.
Local finalists have also included the world's first fully upcycled skyscraper Quay Quarter Tower, the Sydney Institute of Marine Science's living seawalls project, and an Australian-owned cattle and sheep feed supplement which used seaweed.
Mr Knauf said he hoped the recognition would mean the work of the Indigenous Desert Alliance would be shared worldwide.
"We get our whole global network behind them to scale, replicate their work and really champion what they're doing on a global stage," he said.
"We say that we want our finalist to be the loudest voice in any room that they walk into and we help them to achieve that."

title: El milano real resucita en Extremadura con más de cien ejemplares traídos de Inglaterra
content: El proyecto internacional impulsado por la organización extremeña AMUS logra asentar la especie en el suroeste peninsular tras liberar 126 ejemplares británicos y propicia su histórico regreso como reproductor al sur de PortugalEcologistas denunciarán a la Junta de Extremadura en Bruselas por ampliar la caza en Monfragüe y poner en peligro al águila imperial y al buitre negro La población de milano real en el suroeste de la Península Ibérica muestra signos de recuperación tras años en situación crítica. En 2020, la presencia de esta rapaz, catalogada 'En Peligro de Extinción' en España, se limitaba a entre dos y tres parejas reproductoras en la comarca pacense de la Sierra Suroeste. Hoy, los datos del programa LIFE Eurokite, liderado por la organización conservacionista extremeña AMUS (Acción por el Mundo Salvaje), confirman la consolidación de 11 parejas reproductoras y el nacimiento de siete pollos en la zona durante la campaña de 2026. Este incremento poblacional se debe a las liberaciones realizadas entre 2022 y 2025, periodo en el que se trasladaron 126 ejemplares procedentes de Inglaterra mediante la colaboración entre entidades españolas y británicas. Según detallan desde AMUS, los resultados obtenidos este año superan las previsiones iniciales del proyecto. Nidos entre Badajoz, Huelva y el Alentejo portugués La distribución de los asentamientos refleja la fijación progresiva de la especie en el territorio. El núcleo principal se sitúa a menos de diez kilómetros del punto de liberación, con siete parejas establecidas en los términos pacenses de Oliva de la Frontera, Valencia del Mombuey y Zahínos. Otras tres parejas se ubican en un radio de entre 10 y 20 kilómetros, dos en Encinasola (Huelva) y una en Amareleja (Portugal), mientras que una undécima pareja se ha localizado a unos 100 kilómetros, en el municipio de Aljucén. Un milano real sobrevuela el suroeste peninsular El caso de Amareleja supone la confirmación del retorno del milano real como especie reproductora al sur de Portugal, donde se consideraba extinguido en esta faceta desde hacía más de una década y permanece catalogado bajo la máxima categoría de amenaza ('Críticamente en Peligro'). Asimismo, el análisis de los nidos arroja que cinco de las 11 parejas están formadas exclusivamente por ejemplares liberados, mientras que las seis restantes combinan un individuo reintroducido con otro de origen desconocido. Desde AMUS señalan que la presencia fija de los milanos liberados está sirviendo como “reclamo” para atraer a otros ejemplares dispersos por la península, lo que acelera el asentamiento y favorece la diversidad genética. Ecoturismo en 2027 Dado que el milano real alcanza la madurez reproductora entre los dos y tres años, la organización prevé que la población continúe aumentando en los próximos ejercicios. Los ejemplares liberados en 2024 y 2025 se incorporarán a la reproducción entre 2027 y 2028, lo que permitirá incrementar la productividad. Aunque el marco del programa europeo LIFE Eurokite concluye a finales de 2026, AMUS mantendrá el seguimiento sobre el terreno mediante dispositivos GPS con el objetivo de consolidar una población estable de entre 20 y 25 parejas reproductoras. Además, la entidad proyecta poner en marcha en 2027 un programa de turismo de naturaleza centrado en la observación de la especie para generar un impacto económico positivo en los municipios de la zona. El veneno y las líneas eléctricas: los principales riesgos A pesar de la evolución positiva, la entidad advierte de que persisten los factores de riesgo que provocaron el declive de la especie. Aunque el trabajo conjunto con las empresas eléctricas ha permitido adaptar tendidos e impedir episodios graves de electrocución o colisión en la área del proyecto, el uso ilegal de cebos envenenados sigue siendo una amenaza relevante para las rapaces. Por ello, AMUS insiste en la necesidad de mantener la colaboración con el Seprona y la administración ambiental. La iniciativa ha contado con el apoyo de entidades como Endesa, Mossy Earth, la Diputación de Badajoz, Saeta Yield, la Fundación Biodiversidad, Rewilding Europe, Iberia, la Fundación Banco Santander y KITE Optics, además de diversos municipios de España, Portugal y Reino Unido.

title: Day of Countryside Living organizer says rural life best suits active people
content:
Day of Countryside Living organizer says rural life best suits active people
Reve Lambur, the lead organizer of Day of Countryside Living, said that anyone interested in rural life should definitely go meet the vibrant communities who are eager to welcome new residents.
Rural living is best suited for active people, because there are so many opportunities to create something new yourself, she added.
"There are two ideas behind organizing Day of Countryside Living. One is to show that living in the countryside is very pleasant, and to give people who have thought about moving there a chance to see what the local community is like — whether there is work, whether there is housing," said coordinator Reve Lambur.
The second idea is to show local residents what their municipality looks like. "Maybe new people have moved in — it's a chance to introduce them to the community, and for the community to feel proud of their municipality, to see that it's such a great place to live," Lambur said.
This year, 26 rural municipalities are participating. "In previous years, the municipality itself had to be the main contact point, but this year communities could take the lead as well, so we wouldn't take away the opportunity from communities that are actively looking for new residents," Lambur said.
The pandemic, she noted, encouraged many people to move to the countryside — and stay. "Many of them are families with children, because rural living is safe. The downside is that services aren't always close at hand. Families definitely need a car. When visiting communities, you can ask directly about the pros and cons of living there," Lambur explained.
"You don't just move into a house — you move into a community. That's the message of the day. Rural life suits active people. There are so many opportunities to create and do things yourself, to become a spark‑person — someone whose actions matter to others," Lambur said.
This year's Day of Countryside Living will take place on September 19.

Internacional: un programa que busca mejorar 500.000 hectáreas comienza a pagar a productores
EL CALAFATE.- A través de un programa de ganadería regenerativa desarrollado para Sudamérica buscan que los productores agropecuarios puedan regenerar sus tierras, recuperar la biodiversidad y capturar carbono a la par de obtener un ingreso económico. Se trata del programa SARA, que anunció la primera emisión de créditos de carbono verificados por Verra, la principal entidad global de certificación.
El Programa SARA (South American Regenerative Agriculture) es uno de los proyectos pioneros bajo la metodología VM0042, que valida su impacto ambiental, social y económico en la región, y tiene un objetivo ambicioso: aspira a mejorar más de 500.000 hectáreas proyectadas hacia 2028, entre la Argentina, Chile y Paraguay.
“SARA es uno de los primeros siete programas del mundo en ser validados bajo esta metodología y el más grande en Sudamérica en emitir créditos de carbono”, informaron a través de un comunicado difundido por Ovis 21.

title: Australia claims it is a global pioneer in preventing online harm – should other countries follow suit?
content:
Statesmen, shysters, dictators. Over the years, the United Nations has seen all kinds of world leaders.
But when he arrives in New York on Monday for the annual general assembly, Anthony Albanese will be looking for collaborators.
Determined to rein in the power of social media giants harming the lives of children, the Australian prime minister believes only a concerted effort by countries around the world will be enough to force change.
Attending the UN leaders week in September last year, Albanese hosted a stylish event in a room overlooking the East River, talking up Australia’s world-leading moves to ban children under 16 from having social media accounts.
That day, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the world was watching Australia. There to hear from families of children who had taken their own lives after online bullying, the leaders of Greece, Fiji, Tonga and Malta agreed it was time for change.
A year later, the ban is responsible for the closure of as many as 5m accounts in Australia. And, as countries as diverse as France, Brazil and Indonesia follow suit, Albanese is taking the next step.
Earlier this month he announced plans to legislate a digital duty of care, and rules to allow social media users to opt out of the powerful algorithms splintering communities, overheating political debates and targeting vulnerable people.
“We took action because the community said ‘enough was enough’, and we would no longer let Australian kids be treated as commodities instead of children,” Albanese said, anticipating a fight domestically and on the world stage.
Australia, a middle power and a long way from many of the world’s big diplomatic questions, is portraying itself as the leader in tackling big tech’s reach into all our lives.
Albanese believes he is helping spur “a global movement” for change, using public pressure, big fines and diplomacy to correct harm playing out online, as well as in the real world.
“Australia is working to prevent online harm, particularly for our children, and I am proud that Australia is setting the world standard for digital safety,” he said on Friday.
As he flies to the US, where one of his first stops will be at Apple’s California headquarters for talks with its chair and former chief executive, Tim Cook, Albanese will be buoyed up by polling showing two-thirds of voters (66%) support opt out requirements for algorithms. A DemosAU poll this week found only 13% were opposed to the plan.
The majority of respondents believed social media companies should be legally required to reduce foreseeable risks to users, even if it meant more restrictions on their business models.
But the polling is set against a parallel, less positive conversation about AI and Australia’s datacentre boom, with growing disquiet among communities exposed to the country’s 160-odd datacentres and about how they will be powered. To feed the AI that depend on those developments, Albanese appears open to negotiating trading Australian copyright protections in order to do business with the same companies he has taken to task over social media.
In the digital safety space, Tama Leaver, a professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth, says Australia has shown a level of leadership not always expected from a smaller country.
“It is something that gives them a level of credibility, even if the world-leading nature of some of these plans might be slightly overstated,” he told Guardian Australia.
Leaver points to the Netherlands, where a legal challenge found Meta was not compliant with the European Union’s Digital Services Act.
A court ordered the company to add an easily accessible option for Facebook and Instagram users to block algorithmic recommendations, backed up by fines. Even by European standards, Dutch social media users have more power to shape their feeds.
Similarly, last month, Meta agreed to a US$18bn settlement with state governments across America to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. Meta will also implement a suite of changes to better protect children online, including default daily time limits and night-time blocks.
Labor sources describe the government’s online safety push as part of Albanese’s view of Australian leadership in an uncertain world. Acting with key partners, harnessing the concerns of parents and showing that even small countries can have an outsized voice when they’re prepared to lead.
Albanese, and his communications minister, Anika Wells, want to strengthen the coalition of support.
Wells says the wealthy owners of platforms including Google, Meta, TikTok and Snapchat have been “running real-time, unregulated product testing on Australians” for too long.
“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she says.
Under the next round of reforms, users over 16 will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with fines of more than A$100m for platforms breaking the rules. The rules have been dubbed “my feed, my way”.
Children under 18 will be given new protections from specific harms, shielding them from pornography; posts promoting or encouraging eating disorders; misogynistic content; depictions of crime and dangerous stunts; and content likely to cause mental health problems, including abuse and bullying.
Wells is also targeting so-called “nudify apps”, which create fake naked images. Regulators say this kind of abuse has grown more than fivefold since 2019.
“We must move the burden of reporting online harm from the shoulders of victims and stop that harm at the source,” Wells says.
“We must hold big tech accountable for the tools they are creating and putting out to market, including to children.”
But the draft legislation has had a difficult rollout.
The Coalition says Labor is trying to give itself huge powers to censor conservative voices online, with insufficient checks and balances. The Greens, on whom Labor will rely to pass the laws through parliament, say the plan isn’t strong enough. Instead of opt-out ability, they want Australians to proactively opt in to algorithms.
And political risk is waiting for Albanese in the US, too. The White House flagged possible pressure on Australia to stop targeting US-owned tech companies, saying Donald Trump’s administration would raise concerns with trading partners.
Labor has pledged to take time to consult, with the legislation expected to be introduced before Christmas. Albanese will discuss the plans on a series of overseas trips planned before the end of the year: after the UN, he will attend meetings of Commonwealth leaders, as well as the Asean and Apec blocs and the G20 in December.
While Australia’s social media ban has been watched around the world, in the 10 months since it came into effect, questions have been raised about its effectiveness.
Research has found more than 80% of teens under 16 were still on social media following the ban. The government has passed laws to double the fines, and give the eSafety commissioner new powers to investigate compliance.
Even if not completely effective, Greece, Britain and Denmark are advancing plans for similar bans, while restrictions already exist in countries including China, Indonesia and Malaysia.
In a major speech this week, von der Leyen said it was time for Europe to follow Australia, proposing a new “EU Kids Act”.
“I am aware that many perceive the power of big tech as overwhelming. And impossible to roll back,” she said. “I disagree.”
The Australian eSafety commissioner’s office told a parliamentary committee last month that the ban “seeks to unwind more than 20 years of entrenched industry practice”.
Wayne Holdsworth, father of Mac – a teen sextortion victim who took his own life – told the parliament that it would take three to five years to determine the ban’s success.
“We have handed a poisoned chalice to our children that is dangerous and has had a significant negative impact on our kids – in some cases, fatal,” he said.
“When seatbelts were introduced in the late 1970s, some adults didn’t wear them, because it creased their shirt as they threw their cigarette out the window whilst balancing their can of beer on their lap.”
Jason Trethowan, chief executive of the youth mental health organisation Headspace, said: “You have to start somewhere.
“You have to put a line in the sand and then work towards getting those percentages down. And it’ll be a positive.”
Dr Rob Nicholls, a senior researcher associate at the University of Sydney’s centre for AI, trust and governance, said the ban would probably work better over time – particularly as the 13 to 15-year-olds who had social media before the ban aged out of it.
Nicholls said the Albanese government could help other countries follow in its footsteps.
“It’s great to get on a plane to New York to skite about ‘leading’,” he said. “I think that the fast followers of the Australian lead will use the issues that have been found here to hone their legislative approaches.”
And Australia need not seek to lead in all facets of social media regulation globally.
“Australia is best served by sharing the lead with other middle powers, even if we thought of it first.”
Trethowan believes if the changes work, Australia will empower other countries to demand similar features from platforms.
“I think the technology companies are having to defend themselves or make changes to their algorithms and the way in which they design features to mitigate their potential fines,” he said.
“Australia’s set it up for other countries to take on similar things.”

title: Park rangers rescue days-old elephant after she was separated from her mother and hid among a herd of zebras for safety
content:
Since 1977, the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has been a leading conservation organization in East Africa. Across Nairobi National Park and Tsavo East National Park, it operates the most successful orphan elephant rescue and rehabilitation program in the world.
By working with the Kenya Wildlife Service, the nonprofit rescues distressed elephants, as well as rhinos, giraffes, lions, leopards, and more. When reunification isn’t possible, the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust provides sanctuary for animals in need, always with the goal of returning them to the wild.
On November 4, 2025, the Kenya Wildlife Service received reports of an orphaned elephant sighting in Tsavo East, “a place of open skies and big predators.”
“Tourists had spotted her, alone and with no other elephants in the area,” the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust stated on its website. “Several hours had elapsed since the sighting, but fortunately the tour driver had pinned the location of the tiny elephant.”
Trevor, a Tsavo works manager, led a search party with a team of field agents through the Wangalla plains. After a little more than an hour, they finally found her “deep in the bush,” huddling among a herd of zebras.
“Frightened and desperate, she had latched onto the closest creatures who could provide company and protection,” the nonprofit explained.
“It was a heartbreaking scene: The little calf was visibly distressed, crying and pacing in search of her mother. The team extensively looked for her family, but there were no other herds in the area.”
According to the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, wildlife officials believe that the calf’s family had been scared off by a pack of lions that had been hunting buffalo the night prior. In the confusion, she was likely separated from her own herd and had journeyed too far to find them again.
“It’s a miracle she survived the night on her own; a calf so small would be easy prey for the lions, jackals, and hyenas who prowl under cover of darkness,” the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust said.
After she was rescued, the calf was transported by vehicle and then by helicopter to the Kaluku Field Headquarters and Neonate Nursery.
“We named the orphan Wangalla, to connect her to her origins,” the nonprofit said. “Barely a week old, we knew that we had a challenge on our hands — a challenge for one of our most experienced keepers.”
Wangalla was paired with Misheck, an elephant care team member who had first joined the organization in 1998, when he was 22 years old. In the decades since, he had become the go-to keeper for orphaned elephants.
“Wangalla fell fully and completely in love with Misheck — and the feeling was mutual. He has been extraordinarily committed to this little elephant, spending nearly every minute of every day by her side. Despite our many pleas that he take a well-earned break, he refused to take leave for a full five months after her rescue.”
According to the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, whenever Misheck was asked if he needed a break, he would always reply: “There is nowhere else I would rather be.”
Today, Wangalla is 10 months old. She still spends her evenings with Misheck, who hand-plucks leaves for her to eat at sunset.
During the day, she plays among the guineafowl at the sanctuary and dusts herself near Musumbi, the hippo’s, pool. She has also joined the social circle of the sanctuary’s older elephants, joining them for walks and running between their legs.
“In the fullness of time, Wangalla’s journey will take her back to the wilds of Tsavo East, where her story began,” the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust wrote. “But now, this remarkable little elephant has a family with us, in the bosom of the birds, the elephants, and the extraordinary keepers that make Kaluku home.”

title: Colombia’s Constitutional Court Bans the Use of Animals for Tourist Traction Activities
content:
Colombia’s Constitutional Court has declared unconstitutional an exception that allowed animals to be used in traction vehicles for tourism and recreational activities. The decision, issued through Ruling C-310 of 2026, changes the scope of Law 2138 of 2021 and directly affects practices such as traditional horse-drawn carriages used for tourist tours in some cities across the country.
The ruling was issued on September 23, 2026, after the Court’s Plenary Chamber reviewed a constitutional challenge concerning the word “tourist,” included in Paragraph 2 of Article 2 of Law 2138. The law established a replacement system for animal-drawn vehicles but maintained an exception for those associated with tourism services.
According to the Court, the exception is contrary to Article 79 of the Colombian Constitution, which recognizes the right to enjoy a healthy environment and to participate in decisions that may affect it. The Court determined that the recreational or tourism-related nature of an activity does not provide sufficient constitutional justification for continuing to use animals when doing so may cause unnecessary suffering.
Colombia’s Constitutional Court removes tourism exception, with six-month transition period
Although the Court struck down the exception, the decision will not take effect immediately. The Court determined that the declaration of unconstitutionality will be deferred for six months from the notification of the ruling, giving local authorities time to prepare the mechanisms needed to implement the replacement process.
During this period, mayors’ offices and departmental governments will have to develop programs to replace animal-drawn vehicles used for tourism activities. The decision also includes measures for job retraining for people whose income is connected to the activity, meaning the transition will involve more than removing animals from tourist services.
The ruling also extended the declaration of unconstitutionality to other provisions related to the same issue through the integration of the relevant legal provisions. These include Article 10 of Law 2138 of 2021 and Paragraph 1 of Article 98 of Law 769 of 2002, Colombia’s National Traffic Code.
The decision will apply nationwide and require authorities to establish mechanisms to replace this form of tourist transportation. The six-month period granted by the Court is intended to facilitate planning, the implementation of alternatives, and protections for workers who currently depend on tours involving animals.
Cartagena, one of the most relevant cases in the transition
Cartagena is particularly relevant to the discussion because traditional tourist carriages were part of the Historic Center’s tourism offering for decades. The city had already begun its own transition before the Constitutional Court issued its national ruling.
In December 2025, the Cartagena mayor’s office issued Decree 2296, which banned the circulation of animal-drawn carriages in the Historic Center and the walled area. The measure was accompanied by the introduction of electric carriages to replace horse-drawn vehicles.
The district government later reported that the electric tourist carriage system began operating on December 30, 2025, and that 120 horses were removed from tourism activities. The animals entered a retirement and responsible adoption process, with the condition that they would not be used again for work, commercial activities, or recreational purposes.
Cartagena’s transition followed several years of debate. In 2020, during the national discussion over replacing animal-drawn vehicles, representatives of the city proposed replacing tourist carriages with electric alternatives while maintaining the source of income for carriage operators.
In 2024, the District Council also considered a proposal for a pilot program involving 10 colonial-style electric vehicles for tourism purposes. The initiative proposed a negotiated transition aimed at maintaining the economic activity while eliminating the use of horses.
The city government also held discussions with carriage and horse owners to establish employment and operational alternatives. In December 2025, the administration said the options included horse adoption, defining routes, and possible mechanisms for incorporating workers into positions with the district government.
Other cities have also advanced in the replacement process
The elimination of animal-drawn vehicles did not begin with the 2026 ruling. Several municipalities had previously developed replacement programs, although not all were specifically related to tourism.
In Popayán, for example, the municipal administration began a process to replace animal-drawn vehicles in 2022. The city government later reported progress toward eliminating horse-drawn carts and said the process included alternatives for families that depended on the activity. In December 2023, the municipality also issued a decree banning the circulation of animal-drawn vehicles throughout the city.
In Cartagena, meanwhile, the discussion has been closely tied to tourism and the challenge of preserving a traditional activity without continuing to use animals. The city’s experience provides an example of the type of transition that other local authorities will now have to develop.
The ruling creates a new framework for animal-drawn tourist transportation in Colombia. During the six-month transition period, authorities will have to determine how to replace these vehicles, establish job retraining mechanisms, and ensure that animals removed from the activity are not returned to tourist work.

title: Ηλεκτρονικά τιμολόγια: Ποιοι πρέπει να τρέξουν στην ΑΑΔΕ έως 12 Οκτωβρίου
content:
Διευκρινίσεις ενόψει της υποχρεωτικής ηλεκτρονικής τιμολόγησης παρέχει η ΑΑΔΕ, ξεκαθαρίζοντας ποιοι πρέπει να υποβάλουν τη «Δήλωση Έναρξης Ηλεκτρονικής Έκδοσης Στοιχείων» και ποιοι μπορούν να συνεχίσουν προσωρινά να εκδίδουν τιμολόγια με τους υφιστάμενους τρόπους. Η δήλωση αφορά αποκλειστικά τις επιχειρήσεις με ακαθάριστα έσοδα έως 1.000.000 ευρώ, με βάση το φορολογικό έτος 2023, οι οποίες επιλέγουν την περίοδο προσαρμογής από την 1η Οκτωβρίου έως το τέλος του 2026.
Συγκεκριμένα, με το ισχύον κανονιστικό πλαίσιο (Α.1128/2025, Β΄ 4937 και Α.1129/2025, Β΄ 4938), η συγκεκριμένη δήλωση απαιτείται στις ακόλουθες περιπτώσεις:
– Για την παροχή κινήτρων λόγω πρόωρης εφαρμογής της ηλεκτρονικής τιμολόγησης (άρθρ. 71Θ, παρ. 1 ΚΦΕ), κατά το διάστημα που αυτά ίσχυαν.
– Για τη δυνατότητα σταδιακής συμμόρφωσης των υπόχρεων οντοτήτων, με παράλληλη χρήση των υφιστάμενων τρόπων έκδοσης παραστατικών.
Τι ισχύει από 1/10/2026
Η υποβολή της δήλωσης, η οποία δύναται να λάβει χώρα έως 12/10/2026, απαιτείται πλέον αποκλειστικά από επιχειρήσεις με ακαθάριστα έσοδα έως 1.000.000 ευρώ, με βάση το φορολογικό έτος 2023, οι οποίες επιθυμούν να κάνουν χρήση της περιόδου προσαρμογής, από 1/10/2026 έως 31/12/2026, και να συνεχίσουν παράλληλα να εκδίδουν τα τιμολόγιά τους και με τους υφιστάμενους τρόπους.
Αντιθέτως αν από 1/10/2026 οι επιχειρήσεις ήδη εκδίδουν αποκλειστικά τα τιμολόγιά τους μέσω των εφαρμογών timologio ή myDATAapp, δεν απαιτείται η υποβολή «Δήλωσης Έναρξης Ηλεκτρονικής Έκδοσης Στοιχείων».
Σημειώνεται ότι τα ανωτέρω αφορούν την υποβολή δήλωσης σχετικά με τη χρήση των εφαρμογών timologio ή myDATAapp και δεν επηρεάζουν την υποχρέωση υποβολής δήλωσης για τη χρήση Υπηρεσιών Παρόχου Ηλεκτρονικής Τιμολόγησης όπως ορίζεται στην απόφαση του Διοικητή της ΑΑΔΕ (Α.1112/2025, Β’ 4206).
Ταυτόχρονα, η εφαρμογή της υποχρεωτικής ηλεκτρονικής τιμολόγησης δεν επιφέρει καμία αλλαγή στις υποχρεώσεις και τον τρόπο έκδοσης των παραστατικών εσόδων στις συναλλαγές με τελικούς καταναλωτές, δηλαδή στις λιανικές συναλλαγές.
Η δήλωση, στις περιπτώσεις που απαιτείται, υποβάλλεται μέσω της ψηφιακής πύλης myAADE (myaade.gov.gr), στη διαδρομή: Εφαρμογές > Φορολογικές Υπηρεσίες > myDATA > Δήλωση ηλεκτρονικής έκδοσης στοιχείων μέσω Παρόχου, ΙδιοΠαρόχου ή της εφαρμογής timologio.

title: Scientists identify 'sweet spot' for early stage of life on Earth that preceded LUCA, the ancestor of all living things
content:
Scientists identify 'sweet spot' for early stage of life on Earth that preceded LUCA, the ancestor of all living things
New research has pinned down the onset of the "RNA World," a hypothetical time in Earth's very early history when RNA was the primary replicating substance.
Scientists have identified a "sweet spot" in Earth's deep past when conditions were optimal for a proposed early stage of life to take hold — a phase known as the RNA World.
The sweet spot was 4.33 billion years ago, although Earth may have become suitable for the RNA World as early as 4.4 billion years ago, given that extreme bombardment by asteroids, comets and other rocky leftovers of planet formation had largely stopped by then, the researchers reported in a study published Tuesday (Sept. 22) in the journal Nature Communications.
The findings give a more precise estimate of the RNA World's onset than previous studies based on geochemical modeling, biomolecular analyses and simulations of early atmospheric chemistry did, study first author Oleg Abramov, a senior scientist at the Arizona-based Planetary Science Institute, told Live Science in an email.
"The timing is consistent with previous estimates of approximately 4.35 billion years ago, but our range of uncertainty is significantly narrower," Abramov explained, adding that "previous ranges included 4.46 to 4.26 billion years ago, and 4.45 to 3.9 billion years ago."
The RNA World is a hypothetical time in Earth's history before the emergence of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA), the single microbe from which all living things on Earth descend. RNA, or ribonucleic acid, is a single-stranded molecule that is structurally similar to DNA and performs vital functions in living cells. Scientists think the RNA World preceded the emergence of DNA; in that early epoch, RNA would have been the primary replicating substance, carrying genetic information across generations of basic lifeforms by copying itself independently.
RNA evolved into its more chemically stable cousin, DNA, sometime before the emergence of LUCA. Scientists think the RNA World first developed into an RNA-and-protein world, and that DNA then appeared in two distinct stages nicknamed the U-DNA and T-DNA worlds.
While researchers have suggested alternative and hybrid scenarios for the emergence of life on Earth, the RNA World is a leading hypothesis, Abramov said. To determine when it might have existed, he and his colleagues built a computer model of Earth's interior that simulated how giant impacts on the planet's surface between 4.5 billion and 3.5 billion years ago affected conditions in the crust and Earth's overall compatibility with life.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"We constructed an impact bombardment model constrained by observables such as the lunar cratering record," Abramov said. "We examined both detrimental effects of impacts, such as temperature-induced degradation of key biomolecules, and effects conducive to life, such as generation of hydrothermal systems."
The model showed that space rocks measuring hundreds of miles across — an order of magnitude larger than the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, but far smaller than the impactor that created the moon — went on slamming into Earth and sterilizing its surface until 4.4 billion years ago. Life could not have survived such intense bombardment, which probably triggered widespread melting of the crust, ocean vaporization, extreme temperature gradients in the crust and continuous showers of burning material and rock-vapor rain at the surface, Abramov said.
However, the conditions stabilized after 4.4 billion years ago. And as a result, hydrothermal vent clusters appeared within the near-surface crust that concentrated the ingredients for RNA, including nucleotides, short amino-acid chains called peptides and fat-like compounds known as lipids, Abramov said.

- 'RNA can do things which we have never seen before': New study challenges assumptions about what RNA was up to at the dawn of life
- Scientists discover first direct evidence that slivers of 'proto-Earth' may survive today
- Scientist accidentally stumbles across bizarre ancient ‘wrinkle structures’ in Morocco that shouldn't be there
"These criteria point to the Earth becoming suitable for an RNA World between 4.4 and 4.3 billion years ago, with optimal conditions at approximately 4.33 billion years ago," he said.
The results suggest there was a gap of roughly 130 million years between the heyday of the RNA World and the emergence of LUCA, which scientists think lived about 4.2 billion years ago. However, there are still large uncertainties around both events, so the interval could be as big as 240 million years, Abramov noted.
"The duration of the RNA World is highly uncertain, and our study did not explicitly constrain it," he said.
Abramov, O., Medvegy, A., Kremer, B. and Mojzsis, S. J. (2026). A Hadean timeline for the emergence of the RNA World. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76978-3
Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

title: How Akagera ended big five poaching
content: For more than a decade, not a single elephant, lion or rhino has been poached in Akagera National Park, marking a major conservation milestone after 15 years of sustained anti-poaching efforts. The campaign has helped more than double the park's large mammal population, from 4,476 in 2010 to 11,338 in 2023, according to park data, underscoring one of Rwanda's most remarkable wildlife recovery stories. Once on the brink due to rampant poaching and human pressure, Rwanda's only savannah national park has transformed into a thriving conservation area. ALSO READ: Akagera park named among world’s top 25 destinations Following the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, Akagera was reduced to about two-thirds of its original size to accommodate returning Rwandans. Today, more than 500,000 people live along its boundaries, increasing pressure on land and natural resources. For years, many residents relied on the park for bushmeat and income, driving widespread poaching. Park officials say reversing the trend required far more than armed patrols. According to Jean Paul Karinganire, Akagera National Park's Funding and Reporting Manager, the park's recovery has been driven by sustained ranger patrols, intelligence-led operations, snare removal, stronger law enforcement, fencing, community engagement and investment in tourism. The communities living around the park have developed a strong sense of ownership of its ecosystem. Through annual tourism revenue-sharing, development projects are implemented in their communities, creating new opportunities. Wildlife recovery is also the result of years of intensive anti-poaching measures, including ranger patrols, snare removal, community intelligence networks, fencing and stronger law enforcement, Karinganire said. He noted that nearly 2,000 wire snares had been removed from the park by 2012 through community engagement campaigns. Today, only a small number are recovered each year, reflecting a sharp decline in illegal hunting. The improved security has enabled the reintroduction of species that had disappeared due to poaching and conflict. Lions returned in 2015 and 2017, black rhinos in 2017 and 2019, and white rhinos in 2021 and 2025, restoring Akagera's Big Five. Former poachers embrace new livelihoods One of those helping protect the park today is Issa Ntakiyimana, a former poacher who now leads the Tubungabunge Urusobe rw'Ibinyabuzima Cooperative in Murama Sector, Kayonza District. After witnessing fellow poachers lose their lives during illegal hunting expeditions, Ntakiyimana abandoned poaching and began encouraging others to do the same. In 2023, he and five colleagues launched a door-to-door campaign urging poachers to surrender their weapons and traps. Within months, nearly 60 former poachers had joined the initiative. ALSO READ: How Akagera Park’s Rwf1.2bn community fund will be spent After raising awareness, we handed over eight spears, seven bows and 25 traps previously used to hunt buffaloes and antelopes, Ntakiyimana said. The group also worked with park rangers to recover wire snares, makeshift camps and cooking equipment hidden inside the park. Today, cooperative members earn a living through farming instead of poaching. Local authorities allocated two hectares for food crops and another 30 hectares for coffee cultivation, while members also established a savings and loan scheme to support small businesses. Communities around the park now understand the importance of protecting the ecosystem. Conservation has become everyone's responsibility, and we have taken ownership of it, Ntakiyimana said. The wildlife recovery has also boosted Akagera's tourism industry. The park now attracts more than 51,700 paying visitors annually and generates over $5 million in revenue each year. Domestic tourists account for about 60 percent of visitors, while surrounding communities benefit through jobs, procurement opportunities, tourism revenue-sharing and a five percent Special Guarantee Fund that compensates residents for certain wildlife-related damage. Established in 1934, Akagera National Park covers 1,122 square kilometres across Kayonza, Gatsibo and Nyagatare districts in eastern Rwanda. It is home to the Big Five and more than 500 wildlife species, including hundreds of bird species.

title: WaveFoG: Wavelet Gated Transformer for Parkinson's Freezing of Gait Detection Using Wearable Accelerometer Signals
content: Freezing of gait (FoG) is one of the most debilitating episodic motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). FoG detection from wrist worn inertial signals poses challenging problems such as extreme data class imbalance (only 12-18% of signal windows are FoG), low frequency postural instabilities alongside diagnostically crucial 3-8 Hz rhythmic tremors, and the need for subject independent generalisation. To address these, this paper presents WaveFoG, a novel wavelet gated Transformer architecture that combines multi scale representations from discrete wavelet transform (DWT) with a dual branch encoder. A 1D CNN captures local gait texture, and a Transformer captures global temporal context. They are fused via a sigmoid gating fusion layer that modulates the encoder output based on the DWT sub-band descriptors. Trained with focal loss and evaluated on the public Kaggle TLVMC FoG Prediction dataset under subject independent grouped ten fold cross validation (SI-CV), WaveFoG achieves a mean F1-score of 0.875 +/- 0.017 and AUPRC of 0.833 +/- 0.020, exceeding single branch baselines (1D CNN, Bi-LSTM, and vanilla Transformer) by up to 5.4 pp on F1. Temporal saliency maps highlight temporal patterns that are consistent with reported characteristics of FoG onset. The source code of this project is available at: https://github.com/Shihabul-Shuvo/WaveFoG

title: Chile's Atacama Desert blossoms with life after El Niño rains
content:
A display of flowers has bloomed across Chile's Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, after the El Niño climate phenomenon brought heavy rain to the region.
Beneath the normally parched ground, millions of seeds and bulbs from around 200 species lie in wait for water.
Heavy rain associated with El Niño recently lashed northern Chile, prompting the plants to emerge.
Now, violet flowers carpet vast stretches of the desert, and white buds peek out from the cracked ground.
Dozens of tourists pull over to snap pictures of the scenery, which, with any luck, might even include a rainbow against a deep red sunset.
Seasonal rainfall of more than 180 millimeters (7 inches) in some areas "had never been recorded before," Cesar Pizarro, head of Atacama biodiversity for Chile's forestry body CONAF, told AFP.
Rainfall seeped deeper than usual into the sand, giving new life to the nature reserve about 800 kilometers (500 miles) north of Santiago.
The "flowering desert" phenomenon will peak in October, according to CONAF, which estimates that 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) will bloom.
The current El Niño is predicted to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
The phenomenon raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall, as well as erratic weather conditions.
The torrential rains that pounded Chile in July killed 13 people and destroyed or severely damaged around 4,000 homes.
'Generates life'
While acknowledging those devastating effects, Pizarro also noted that nature can benefit from El Niño.
"Although there is great concern… about the impacts it is causing in many places, it also generates life," he said.
Atacama is witnessing "more than flowers," he added, explaining that insects, snails, birds, reptiles and mammals proliferate, too.
Bees pollinate the flowers, while beetles feast on their leftovers and fertilize the soil with their nitrogen-rich excrement ahead of the next rainfall.
Pizarro hopes a massive influx of tourists won't cause too much damage to the natural haven. He stressed the importance of using established footpaths and leaving pets at home.
"For our country, the flowering desert is a source of pride. It is part of our heritage," he said, admiring the yellow flowers sprouting around him.
"Although there are several deserts that bloom when it rains, the territorial extent and the diversity of species we have here are unique," he said.
