title: Nuevo Centro de Enfermedades No Transmisibles, qué atiende y cómo tener cita
content:
Nuevo Centro de Enfermedades No Transmisibles, qué atiende y cómo tener cita
Evaluaciones médicas, pruebas diagnósticas y seguimiento se concentrarán en un establecimiento que funcionará como enlace entre unidades de salud y hospitales.
El Centro Especializado de Enfermedades No Transmisibles (CENT) atenderá a pacientes con padecimientos crónicos que necesiten evaluación especializada, estudios diagnósticos, tratamiento y seguimiento.
El ministro de Salud, Francisco Alabi, brindó detalles sobre el funcionamiento del CENT durante una entrevista con Canal 10, este 23 de septiembre. Mencionó que el establecimiento funciona como un punto de referencia entre las unidades de salud y los hospitales.
¿Cómo conseguir una cita en el nuevo centro?
El proceso para acceder a la atención comienza en una unidad de salud, donde se identifica el padecimiento y se genera la referencia hacia el Centro Especializado de Enfermedades No Transmisibles.
Posteriormente, el centro evalúa el caso y, si es aceptado, el paciente recibe una notificación directa. Alabi señaló que la notificación se realiza en un lapso de 24 a 48 horas y que la comunicación puede efectuarse por llamada telefónica o mensaje.
Después se agenda la cita y el paciente se presenta al establecimiento para iniciar el proceso de diagnóstico y tratamiento.
Una vez estabilizado, puede regresar a la unidad de salud para continuar su seguimiento y recibir los medicamentos correspondientes, según explicó el funcionario.
¿Qué servicios ofrece el Centro de Enfermedades No Transmisibles?
El establecimiento dispone de médicos especialistas y personal de enfermería, psicología, nutrición, salud mental, radiología, patología, farmacia y administración. Alabi señaló que el centro cuenta con cerca de 100 personas distribuidas entre estas áreas.
Entre las atenciones y estudios mencionados durante la entrevista están:
- Colposcopías
- Ultrasonidos
- Electrocardiogramas
- Ecocardiogramas
- Holter
- Pruebas de esfuerzo
- Mamografías
- Exámenes de laboratorio automatizados
- Evaluaciones de nutrición
- Endocrinología
- Psicología
- Anatomía patológica
Alabi explicó, por ejemplo, que una persona con hipertensión referida desde una unidad de salud puede recibir en el mismo establecimiento evaluación especializada y estudios como electrocardiograma, ecocardiograma, Holter, prueba de esfuerzo y exámenes de laboratorio. Después puede recibir tratamiento y una evaluación de su respuesta antes de regresar al primer nivel de atención.
Atención para cáncer de mama y cervicouterino
Durante la entrevista, el ministro también mencionó servicios relacionados con cáncer cervicouterino y cáncer de mama.
En el caso del cáncer cervicouterino, señaló que el centro dispone de pruebas diagnósticas, colposcopías y equipos para procedimientos de tratamiento. Para cáncer de mama mencionó equipos de mamografía y mamografía con tomosíntesis.
Alabi también indicó que existen estudios para el seguimiento de cáncer de próstata dentro de las atenciones relacionadas con enfermedades crónicas no transmisibles.
¿Qué pasa si un paciente llega con una complicación?
Alabi explicó que si una persona llega descompensada, es referida directamente a un hospital para recibir atención como una emergencia.
Los pacientes que se encuentran en proceso de diagnóstico o de establecimiento de tratamiento y que no presentan una complicación pueden recibir atención en el Centro Especializado de Enfermedades No Transmisibles, según explicó el funcionario.
Centro cuenta con farmacia y laboratorio de anatomía patológica
La inversión reportada para el establecimiento es de aproximadamente $12.6 millones. Según Alabi, $10 millones corresponden a infraestructura y el resto al equipamiento.
El inmueble tiene tres niveles y cuenta con una farmacia especializada. El ministro explicó que también posee un laboratorio automatizado de anatomía patológica, que describió como el primero de este tipo dentro del Ministerio de Salud.
El funcionario señaló que el establecimiento cubre San Salvador y que existe planificación para crear centros en las zonas occidental y oriental del país.

title: How poorly fitted sports bras drive girls out of sports
content:
How poorly fitted sports bras drive girls out of careers
What you need to know:
- Poorly fitted sports bras can cause pain, discomfort and embarrassment, yet schools and sports organisations rarely provide proper breast support.
- Researchers say recognising sports bras as essential sports equipment could improve comfort, confidence and performance.
Australian sport has a participation problem, especially when it comes to girls and women. In fact, Australian girls and women are dropping out of organised sports at concerning rates. There are myriad reasons why this is happening. One barrier that gets little coverage is sports bras.
We recently studied how decision-makers in schools and sports organisations understand breast-related barriers to participation and whether they recognised sports bras as part of the solution.
Why are sports bras so important?
Sports bras are essential for girls and women because breasts move a lot during activities such as running, jumping or quick changes in direction. This movement can cause pain, chafing and embarrassment, which may discourage participation and hurt performance.
A high-support, properly fitted sports bra can alleviate or resolve these issues and allow girls and women to exercise comfortably. However, research shows up to 88 per cent of girls wear sports bras that do not fit properly and only about a third wear a sports bra during PE or school sports.
Not including sports bras in school uniforms or sports kits, and not teaching about bra fit and breast health, are gaps that need addressing. The good news is these gaps can be addressed through practical, achievable changes to assist the health, comfort and performance of girls and women playing sport.
We identified several problems
Our team surveyed 225 people – including coaches, teachers, administrators and programme coordinators – who decide on sports kit items in 153 sporting organisations and 72 schools across Australia.
We identified several key issues: many girls and women do not understand the benefits of supportive sports bras; cost makes it difficult for some to access sports bras, especially in schools and community sports; and sports bras are often seen as underwear instead of performance equipment.
One respondent told us: “In the same way that a mouth guard protects teeth, breasts are high-contact areas in our sport that require protection and support.”
Most respondents said breast-related issues negatively affect participation – a majority believed about 40 per cent of girls and women in their organisations faced breast-related problems that limited participation, led to dropping out and impacted performance.
However, most understood the benefits of sports bras: about 95 per cent believed sports bras help prevent breast pain during exercise, and more than 90 per cent said they reduced embarrassment from too much breast movement.
About 92 per cent of decision-makers thought girls and women would benefit from learning about sports bra design, fit and support. While two-thirds felt their organisation should provide this education, less than one per cent actually offered sports bra education. Only two per cent formally included sports bras in school or sports kits.
We also suggest some solutions
We developed a guide that presents solutions to assist sports and schools in dealing with this problem. It includes facts, free evidence-based resources on sports bras for use in promotional efforts, and case studies on organisations that are educating and supporting girls and women to access sports bras.
Key solutions included schools and sports accepting the responsibility to educate girls and women on the importance of wearing supportive, well-fitted sports bras and recognising sports bras as an essential item in sports kits.
Two case studies also identified recent success stories: At Gilgandra High School in New South Wales, teachers noticed few girls were taking part in sports and found a lack of access to supportive sports bras was a problem. The school used NSW government equity funding to give students professionally fitted sports bras for free.
Also read: What if the bra lets her down?
This led to a 35 per cent increase in girls taking part in the school’s athletics carnival. It also boosted their confidence, comfort and willingness to talk about breast health. Also, the Queensland Academy of Sport added breast health education and sports bra fittings to their athlete support services. A physiotherapist met with athletes one-on-one to explain how sports bra design and fit can improve performance and comfort and help prevent breast injuries.
The academy found its athletes were much more likely to use breast health resources after getting personal advice from trusted health professionals. These sessions also made it easier to talk about breast health and lowered barriers to getting help.
Practical tips for sports and schools
There are several things sporting clubs and schools can do to help: Recognise sports bras as essential equipment for girls and women because breast support is important for keeping them involved in sport; add breast health and sports bra education, along with access to evidence-based resources, to physical education programmes in high schools and women’s sport training sessions; offer opportunities for girls and women to learn about sports bra design and proper fit in supportive settings; and assist with funding or identify where funding could be provided to help make sports bras more affordable.
If we want to boost participation and reduce dropout rates among girls and women, making sure they have access to proper breast support could be one of the easiest and most effective things we do.
Deirdre McGhee is a researcher and senior lecturer at the University of Wollongong and APA sports physiotherapist at the University of Wollongong; Clare Hanlon is a professor and chairperson of Susan Alberti Women in Sport at Victoria University; and Dr Elliott Flowers is a postdoctoral research fellow (Women and Girls in Sport), Victoria University.

title: Un “tesoro oxidado” hallado en Austria ha resultado ser el conjunto de barras de la Edad del hierro más grande encontrado en toda Europa
content:
Un “tesoro oxidado” hallado en Austria ha resultado ser el conjunto de barras de la Edad del hierro más grande encontrado en toda Europa
Arqueología
El conjunto de hace más de 2.000 años habría sido suficiente para forjar aproximadamente 500 espadas
Los trabajos de extracción industrial de grava en Deinham (Austria) tuvieron que detenerse de inmediato. Había algo entre las pequeñas piedras que ponía en peligro todo el engranaje. Enterrados, los trabajadores descubrieron una gran cantidad de objetos de hierro oxidados.
Había tantos que difícilmente se podía tratar de un hecho fortuito. Por eso decidieron ponerse en contacto con los arqueólogos de la Universidad de Innsbruck, que recogieron ese “tesoro oxidado” y se lo llevaron al laboratorio para poder analizarlo al detalle.
Una producción sin precedentes
Lo que descubrieron los expertos austríacos es que ese era el mayor conjunto de barras de la Edad de Hierro hallado nunca en Europa. El alijo pertenecía a la cultura de La Tène, que se localizó en los Alpes y Centroeuropa y abarcó desde mediados del siglo V hasta el siglo I antes de Cristo.
Las piezas prehistóricas eran tan numerosas que apuntan a una producción y un comercio a una escala sin precedentes durante la prehistoria. Los investigadores creen que la cantidad encontrada era suficiente para equipar a unos 500 guerreros con espadas.
Aunque se sabía que el hierro se producía en centros especializados, la magnitud exacta del comercio no se comprende bien, ya que los productos semielaborados de este metal a menudo pasan desapercibidos para quienes los encuentran y son difíciles de datar con precisión.
En la fase final de la Edad del Hierro, Europa experimentó un enorme aumento en la producción de metal, y grandes cantidades y variedades de objetos de hierro se extendieron por todo el continente. El valor de estas barras halladas en Austria debió de ser inmenso, dicen los arqueólogos en un estudio publicado en la revista Antiquity.
“Es poco menos que un pequeño milagro que el mayor hallazgo de barras de hierro prehistóricas de Europa no acabara en manos de chatarreros, sino que se notificara a las autoridades austriacas encargadas de la protección del patrimonio”, dice el profesor Peter Trebsche, autor principal de la investigación.
Trebsche y la doctora Marion Berranger, de la Universidad de Tecnología de Belfort-Montbéliard, analizaron y dataron el hallazgo mediante radiocarbono, concluyendo que hay unos 500 productos semielaborados que suman más de una tonelada de peso.
Es probable que el conjunto se perdiera en un naufragio mientras se transportaba por el río Danubio con fines comerciales, lo que pone de relieve la capacidad de transporte fluvial a gran escala y bien organizado de las sociedades centroeuropeas de la prehistoria tardía.
Se desconoce el destino final de las barras de hierro, pero es probable que se forjaran en Baviera, donde se han hallado varios centros de producción de hierro en las proximidades de los oppida: los emblemáticos asentamientos fortificados de gran tamaño de la Europa de la Edad del Hierro.
Espadas de entre 1,5 y 2 kilos
“Estos productos semielaborados- explica Trebsche- suman alrededor de una tonelada de peso, cantidad suficiente para forjar aproximadamente 500 espadas de entre 1,5 y 2 kg. Incluso teniendo en cuenta la pérdida de material durante la fabricación, habría bastado para armar a un gran grupo de guerreros”.
El periodo de La Tène es conocido por sus grandes tesoros de monedas de oro, como las 443 piezas —que totalizaban 3,7 kg de oro— halladas en el importante oppidum de Manching (Baviera), cerca de una gran zona de extracción de hierro de la que podrían haber procedido las barras austríacas.
“Es plausible”, dicen los expertos de la Universidad de Innsbruck, “que el valor de estas monedas equivaliera al de una tonelada de hierro; por tanto, cabe la posibilidad de que la creciente monetización del periodo de La Tène facilitara transacciones de esta magnitud”.
“Resulta increíble que se transportara una cantidad tan ingente de hierro de una sola vez y que estuviera disponible para una única transacción de intercambio durante la última etapa de la Edad del Hierro. Este hallazgo demuestra la gran capacidad de producción de hierro alcanzada en la región del Danubio durante los siglos III y II antes de Cristo”, concluye Trebsche.

title: Who am I? Self-inquiry as a neurophenomenological approach to consciousness
content: Inconclusive evidence for leading third-person theories of consciousness has renewed scientific interest in its first-person nature. Self-inquiry, a first-person method from Advaita Vedanta, can be operationalized to meet this need, though it has not received prior empirical study, likely owing to Advaita’s idealism. By bracketing Advaita’s metaphysical commitments and mapping its characterization of consciousness onto the distinctions drawn by consciousness science, self-inquiry can be understood as a systematic phenomenology of selfhood. The method’s rationale is that mental contents perpetuate the “narrative self,” or one’s personal identity, so tracing such contents back to the sense of “I” to which they are referred attenuates the narrative self and discloses the “minimal self.” The minimal self is the pre-reflective first-person perspective of experience that carries a sense of “for-me-ness.” Sustained attention to the minimal self may then facilitate a selfless mode of awareness, or nondual awareness, marked by the absence of felt division between self and world. On this account, the narrative self and the appropriative ownership underlying the minimal self are seen as illusory, while an impersonal, reflexive consciousness remains. This deconstruction of selfhood already has neurophenomenological precedent, though from studies confined to Buddhist practice and reliant on idiosyncratic techniques. Self-inquiry thus holds empirical significance: its stepwise structure offers potential reproducibility across participants, a within-practice control, and a target attentional operation whose proposed distinctiveness can be empirically tested. It may also hold clinical relevance, having been proposed for incorporation into psychotherapy amid growing research into the therapeutic potential of self-attenuation.

title: EviStreams: Human-in-the-Loop AI Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews in Medicine
content: Systematic reviews underpin clinical guidelines, yet their data-extraction step is a major expert-labor bottleneck bound by a protocolized workflow: two reviewers extract each study independently, an adjudicator resolves disagreements, and the team keeps an auditable record of how every value was produced. Large language models can assist with extraction, but that assistance must fit established review protocols and preserve reproducibility. We present EviStreams, a live, open-source, no-code web platform that puts review teams in control of AI-assisted extraction at three key stages: program design (a structured decomposition approved before any code runs), field specification (typed field definitions calibrated from a pilot), and extracted predictions (reviewer-blinded dual review with adjudication). Working through a form builder, a domain expert defines typed fields rather than prompts, runs extraction over uploaded PDFs, inspects every value alongside the supporting passage it came from, and resolves a reviewer-blinded dual review into an auditable consensus export. An evaluation across four clinical corpora and three frontier model families, released with the system, shows that extraction quality is shaped far more by the field specification than by the choice of model. EviStreams is live at https://evistreams.com/demo and released under Apache-2.0.

title: Dopo 15 anni in esilio, abbatte il muro costruito per proteggere i suoi libri dal regime di Assad: in Siria riemerge la biblioteca nascosta
content:
Dopo 15 anni in esilio, abbatte il muro costruito per proteggere i suoi libri dal regime di Assad: in Siria riemerge la biblioteca nascosta
Nel tumultuoso scenario del 2011, mmentre la Siria veniva investita dall’ondata di proteste e dalla feroce repressione del regime guidato da Bashar al-Assad, la casa di Damasco di Abu Bilal si trasformò nel teatro di un silenzioso atto di resistenza culturale. Per proteggere una preziosa e pericolosa collezione di volumi considerati espressione di dissenso, opere scientifiche, testi religiosi e documenti personali legati alle recitazioni del Sacro Corano, Abu Bilal prese una decisione drastica.
Con le sue stesse mani, l’uomo costruì una finta parete all’interno dell’abitazione, sigillando ermeticamente scaffali colmi di cultura per sottrarli ai controlli, agli interrogatori e alle persecuzioni della polizia politica. Subito dopo aver completato l’opera di occultamento, Abu Bilal fu costretto a lasciare il Paese alla fine del 2011, trascorrendo circa 15 anni in esilio in Kuwait e separato dai suoi beni più cari, mentre la guerra ridisegnava il volto della nazione. Quella barriera di mattoni divenne così l’unico custode di una memoria collettiva che rischiava di essere spazzata via dalla violenza del conflitto, mentre la nazione sprofondava in una lunga e sanguinosa guerra civile.
La demolizione della parete e la riscoperta della memoria collettiva
A distanza di un decennio e mezzo, in seguito alla caduta del regime, alla fuga di Assad in Russia e all’avvio del nuovo corso politico guidato da Ahmad al-Shara, la famiglia ha potuto finalmente fare ritorno a casa, ritrovando le stanze che la dittatura aveva costretto ad abbandonare. E ora era tempo di far tornare a vivere anche quei libri tanto preziosi. Lo scrittore e attivista siriano Bilal Alloun, figlio di Abu Bilal, ha immortalato in un video emozionante il momento in cui il padre impugnava gli attrezzi per abbattere quel muro eretto quindici anni prima.
Le immagini, condivise sui social media e subito diventate virali, mostrano l’attimo esatto in cui gli scaffali tornano alla luce, svelando libri rimasti miracolosamente intatti nonostante il trascorrere del tempo. La diffusione delle immagini ha riacceso i riflettori non solo sul dramma degli archivi personali dispersi a causa dei conflitti, ma anche sulla resilienza di chi ha scelto di difendere la propria identità culturale a costo di sacrifici enormi. E questa biblioteca ritrovata incarna il simbolo universale della sopravvivenza della memoria e della conoscenza contro gli orrori della censura e dei conflitti politici.

title: Zeca Pagodinho recebe título de embaixador da agricultura urbana por horta em Duque de Caxias (RJ)
content:
A Horta Urbana Xerém I, em Duque de Caxias (RJ), recebeu um importante reconhecimento do governo federal pelo trabalho em prol da segurança alimentar na Baixada Fluminense. O espaço ocupa um terreno de 8 mil metros quadrados cedido pelo cantor e compositor Zeca Pagodinho para produção de alimentos que são destinados às famílias mais vulneráveis da comunidade.
O projeto mantido pelo Instituto Zeca Pagodinho (IZP) produz frutas, legumes e hortaliças para cerca de 10 mil famílias em parceria com o Ministério do Desenvolvimento Agrário e Agricultura Familiar (MDA), a Universidade Federal Rural do Rio (UFRRJ) e a Embrapa Agrobiologia.
De julho de 2025 a junho de 2026, foram colhidas duas toneladas de alimentos que são doados ao Fórum de Cozinhas Solidárias do RJ. A visita do governo federal também marcou uma nova etapa da parceria com o IZP para ampliar o reflorestamento e iniciar a produção de café e cacau em outros 13 mil metros quadrados de terras doadas pelo cantor.
Diante da importância desse trabalho, na última terça-feira (15), uma comitiva do governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) desembarcou em Caxias para conceder a Zeca o título de Embaixador da Agricultura Urbana e Periurbana.
O momento contou com a presença da ministra Fernanda Machiavelli, do Desenvolvimento Agrário e Agricultura Familiar (MDA), e de Wellington Dias, do Desenvolvimento e Assistência Social, Família e Combate à Fome.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
“Hoje estamos aqui para reconhecer o trabalho do cantor e compositor Zeca Pagodinho, como embaixador da agricultura urbana e periurbana no Brasil, ao disponibilizar essa área, organizar a produção e garantir que esses alimentos saudáveis possam chegar para as famílias da região”, declarou a ministra do MDA, Fernanda Machiaveli.
O título de embaixador reconhece de forma simbólica a promoção de hortas comunitárias, quintais agroecológicos urbanos e periurbanos, além da formação de competências locais para produção de alimentos saudáveis, aliando agroecologia, economia solidária e segurança alimentar.
“É um trabalho muito bonito e muito importante para aproximar a produção do consumo, para que a gente consiga de fato trazer a agricultura para perto de quem vive na cidade e para a mesa do povo brasileiro”, completou Machiaveli.

title: RNA Genes Emerge as Hidden Culprits in Inherited Blindness
content:
For decades, the hunt for the genetic causes of retinitis pigmentosa has focused almost exclusively on protein-coding genes, the stretches of DNA that carry the blueprints for the molecular machinery of the retina. Now a team of French researchers has turned the spotlight onto a class of genes that most diagnostic pipelines routinely overlook: the genes that encode small nuclear RNAs, the tiny RNA molecules that help every cell splice its genetic messages into usable form. In a study published in Genome Medicine, the group reports that variants in RNU4-2 or in paralogs of RNU6 account for roughly two percent of individuals with non-syndromic autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in a large national cohort, a finding that reshapes how unsolved blindness cases should be investigated.
Retinitis pigmentosa, also known as rod-cone dystrophy, is one of the most genetically heterogeneous disorders in human medicine. It begins with the progressive loss of rod photoreceptors, the cells responsible for vision in dim light, which produces night blindness and narrowing of the visual field. As the disease advances, cone photoreceptors, which mediate daylight and color vision, degenerate as well, often culminating in severe visual impairment or legal blindness in midlife. Approximately forty genes have so far been linked to the autosomal dominant form of the disease, in which a single inherited copy of a pathogenic variant is sufficient to cause symptoms. Yet even with modern genetic testing, a stubborn fraction of patients never receives a molecular diagnosis.
That diagnostic gap was precisely what motivated the new study. The researchers, led by Isabelle Audo and Christina Zeitz of Sorbonne Université, INSERM, CNRS and the Institut de la Vision in Paris, together with colleagues at the Centre Hospitalier National d’Ophtalmologie des Quinze-Vingts and partner institutions, analyzed a French cohort of 395 families with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa and 418 genetically unsolved cases. Every participant underwent comprehensive ophthalmic examination, including standard-of-care retinal imaging and functional assessments, ensuring that the genetic findings could be interpreted against detailed clinical pictures. The team combined genome sequencing, direct Sanger sequencing and a candidate gene approach to interrogate regions of the genome that standard analyses often skip.
The regions they targeted belong to a family of genes with an unusual biology. Small nuclear RNA genes do not encode proteins; instead, they produce short RNA molecules that form the structural and catalytic core of the spliceosome, the cellular machine that removes intervening sequences from messenger RNA precursors. The U4 and U6 small nuclear RNAs associate with U5 snRNA and a set of proteins to build the tri-small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complex, or tri-snRNP, a central component of the major spliceosome. Because splicing is essential in every cell, one might expect defects in these genes to be lethal or to cause widespread damage. Instead, recent years have revealed a striking pattern: inherited and de novo variants in snRNA genes appear in people with recessive neurodevelopmental disorders, and, as the new work confirms, in people with inherited retinal degeneration.
What makes the retinal findings particularly intriguing is where the disease-causing variants sit within these small RNA genes. The variants associated with retinitis pigmentosa cluster in regions that are distinct from those implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, and they affect domains involved in the assembly of the tri-snRNP with three proteins that retinitis specialists know well: PRPF3, PRPF8 and PRPF31. All three of these proteins are themselves established causes of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. In other words, the retina appears to be exquisitely sensitive to a specific kind of disruption in the splicing machinery, one that interferes with the assembly of the tri-snRNP complex, while other tissues tolerate it. This convergence of RNA genes and spliceosome protein genes on the same disease phenotype provides a coherent mechanistic thread through what had seemed like scattered genetic findings.
The results of the cohort screen were unambiguous. The researchers identified heterozygous inherited variants in RNU4-2 and in RNU6 paralogs in eight unrelated families with non-syndromic autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. In every family where additional members were available for testing, the variant co-segregated with the disease, passing from affected parents to affected children exactly as an autosomal dominant mutation should. None of the affected individuals showed the extra-neurological features that might suggest a syndromal diagnosis; their disease was confined to the retina, reinforcing the idea that these snRNA variants produce a pure retinal phenotype rather than a broader developmental syndrome.
Translated into population terms, the eight families mean that variants in RNU4-2 or RNU6 paralogs account for two percent of the genetically solved individuals with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in the cohort. Perhaps more striking is the comparison the authors draw within the spliceosome category: these snRNA variants represent six percent of all individuals carrying variants in genes coding for the multi-subunit spliceosome complex. A single family of non-coding RNA genes therefore contributes a non-trivial share of the spliceosome-related disease burden, a category that until now has been defined almost entirely by protein-coding genes such as PRPF31, PRPF8, PRPF3, PRPF4, PRPF6, SNRNP200 and RP9. The message for diagnostics is clear: excluding snRNA genes from analysis leaves a measurable fraction of patients without answers.
Why have these genes escaped detection for so long? The answer lies partly in the mechanics of genome analysis. Small nuclear RNA genes are short, repetitive and often present in multiple copies or paralogs scattered across the genome, which complicates the alignment of sequencing reads and the confident calling of variants. Many bioinformatics pipelines are tuned to detect single nucleotide changes in protein-coding exons and simply do not report variants in these loci, even when the underlying sequence data contain them. The French team’s use of genome sequencing combined with targeted Sanger validation illustrates the practical path forward: once a candidate snRNA variant is flagged, conventional sequencing can confirm it and family studies can establish segregation. The bottleneck is not the technology but the willingness to look in places the standard tools ignore.
The clinical implications extend beyond diagnosis. A confirmed molecular diagnosis is the gateway to genetic counseling, allowing affected individuals to understand the inheritance pattern and recurrence risk in their families, and to reproductive options such as preimplantation genetic testing. It is also increasingly the entry ticket to precision therapy, as gene-specific clinical trials for inherited retinal disease multiply. For the two percent of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa patients who carry RNU4-2 or RNU6 paralog variants, inclusion of snRNA genes in diagnostic panels could mean the difference between an unsolved case and eligibility for emerging interventions. The finding also suggests that other unexplained retinal degenerations might owe their existence to additional non-coding RNA genes waiting to be interrogated.
Scientifically, the study strengthens an emerging view of the spliceosome as a hotspot for tissue-specific disease. The retina, with its extraordinarily high metabolic demands and its photoreceptors’ constant need to renew outer segment proteins, appears uniquely vulnerable to partial defects in RNA processing that other tissues can buffer. The clustering of retinal disease variants in tri-snRNP assembly domains, distinct from the regions implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, hints at a genotype-phenotype map within molecules barely a hundred nucleotides long. As genome sequencing becomes the default first test for rare disease, the French cohort results argue that the small RNAs at the heart of the spliceosome deserve a permanent place on the diagnostic checklist, both for the patients they will finally explain and for the biology they continue to reveal.

title: Mejor vigilancia y observación: el legado científico de la erupción del volcán Tajogaite de La Palma
content:
Santa Cruz de Tenerife.- La erupción del volcán Tajogaite, en La Palma (2021) dejó un rastro de destrucción y desolación, pero también un legado científico que se traduce en un refuerzo de las capacidades de vigilancia volcánica, investigación y gestión de los peligros geofísicos.
Cuando se cumplen cinco años del inicio del proceso eruptivo, el Instituto Geográfico Nacional (IGN) destaca que desde entonces ha incorporado nuevas redes de observación, herramientas de inteligencia artificial, sistemas de modelización y nuevas líneas de trabajo en geoquímica y comunicación científica.
Gran impacto
Indica que la experiencia de la erupción tuvo «un gran impacto» dentro del Ministerio de Transportes, que optó por reformar el IGN para que los peligros geofísicos, entre los que se encuentra la actividad volcánica, estuvieran mejor articulados.
Y para ello se creó una estructura específica con una Subdirección General independiente que aborde estos peligros y «mejoró sensiblemente» las condiciones laborales del personal para adecuarlo al trabajo en emergencias, apostando por «una clara profesionalización» del personal especializado en peligros de origen geofísico.
El IGN recuerda también que junto con el Instituto Volcanológico de Canarias (Involcan) ha desarrollado ALERTA CO2, un proyecto pionero en el mundo de vigilancia de gases de origen volcánico, con más de 1.500 sensores que lo convierten en la red más densa de vigilancia de CO2 volcánico del planeta.
Más observación
La erupción del Tajogaite puso de manifiesto la necesidad de disponer de redes de observación más densas, automatizadas y capaces de proporcionar información en tiempo casi real, incide el IGN.
La red sísmica de la isla se había densificado ya en 2021 y sus datos se mantienen abiertos al público para poder ser estudiados por cualquier institución.
Para el control de deformaciones volcánicas se incrementaron las estaciones GNSS e inclinómetros, y se adquirieron imágenes InSAR del satélite PAZ hasta 2024 para generar series temporales y mapas de velocidad.
En 2021 se instaló también un gravímetro relativo que permaneció más de un año.
En geoquímica se desplegaron más de 30 sensores de CO2 desarrollados por el IGN para poder determinar el fenómeno posvolcánico de emanaciones gaseosas antes del desarrollo del proyecto ALERTA CO2.
En geología, el uso del laboratorio del Centro Geofísico de Canarias ha permitido el corte y la clasificación de las rocas por primera vez en una erupción en las islas.
Campañas de campo y análisis sísmico
Desde la erupción se han redoblado las campañas de campo: en geoquímica se inició el muestreo de fumarolas en cráteres, continuando con CO2 en pozos y manantiales, y se han incorporado campañas de flujo difuso; mientras que las campañas RTK de control de deformaciones siguen con su cadencia trimestral.
El análisis sísmico ha experimentado uno de los cambios más significativos desde entonces.
Se han establecido detectores automáticos con técnicas de aprendizaje automático para detectar y analizar de forma más rápida y homogénea la actividad sísmica.
La aplicación a los datos de la erupción generó un catálogo sísmico mucho más completo, permitiendo estudiar con mayor detalle la migración de la sismicidad y la evolución del sistema magmático. La automatización permite además afrontar episodios de elevada actividad donde el análisis manual resulta especialmente exigente, valora el IGN.
También se han desarrollado herramientas de simulación numérica de coladas de lava para análisis de escenarios y simulacros, y se ha trabajado en la automatización de avisos de aviación por emisión de cenizas.
Publicaciones
La información obtenida ha generado 18 publicaciones en revistas internacionales con participación de investigadores del IGN junto a instituciones españolas e internacionales.
Estos trabajos han avanzado en el conocimiento de la estructura profunda del sistema magmático de La Palma, la evolución de sismicidad y deformación, la dinámica eruptiva y la relación entre observables geofísicos y geoquímicos.
La investigación más reciente integra datos petrológicos, geoquímicos y geofísicos para reconstruir los procesos preeruptivos y sineruptivos de la erupción de 2021 en Cumbre Vieja. EFE

title: Cameroon: Cameroon Cotton Farmers Pair Improved Seed With Nature-Based Methods
content:
In Cameroon’s northern cotton belt, growers are combining carefully controlled seed multiplication with trees, crop residue and water-conserving field design to improve yields and withstand dry spells.
A day-old lamb leaps and bleats beneath a shed while, behind a cluster of mud-brick, thatched-roof homes, Akoura Sarki inspects the leaves of his cotton plants for signs of insect damage.
The farmer, now in his late sixties, knows this stage of the season well. About 45 days after planting, growers monitor their fields closely and apply pest controls when needed. For Sarki, however, the quality of the harvest begins much earlier — with the seed.
Sarki is a seed multiplier in Pitoa, about 17 kilometres from Garoua, the capital of Cameroon’s North Region. He is part of a small group of selected farmers who produce first-generation certified seed for wider distribution to commercial cotton growers.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
Cotton farming is a family tradition here, with skills and land often passed from parents to children. Sarki began growing cotton at 15, when he left the family plot to establish a farm of his own. He has now cultivated the crop for more than four decades and is among the about 160 000 farmers contributing to the about 250,721 tonnes of seed cotton and 103,156 tonnes of cotton fibre produced yearly under the authority of the Cameroon Cotton Development Authority (SODECOTON) .
Cameroon is ranked the fifth-largest cotton producer in Africa after West African countries like Benin, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ivory Coast.
Cotton farmers are grouped by sector and zone, with a zonal lead, and belong to the cotton producers’ union (Confédération Nationale des Producteurs de Coton du Cameroun), CNPC-C. The farmers’ confederation organises farming campaigns, negotiates producer prices, and procures major agricultural inputs (such as fertilisers and seeds) for its members.
For the past six years, Sarki has grown the new generation R1 seed on an eight-hectare plot, harvesting about 17 tonnes in a good season. This year, he has expanded the area under cotton to 10 hectares.
Elizabeth Souaibou, another Pitoa farmer, grows cotton on just over a hectare. She has farmed cotton for 10 years and has used R1 seed for six of them.
“Because the bolls contain many seeds and weigh more, we prefer R1,” Souaibou said. “Increased output translates into increased revenue.”
R1 is not a cotton variety but a seed generation, according to Djallo Mana, the zonal chief responsible for the Pomla seed bank in the Gashiga sector. The designation is applied to the first generation of certified seed produced from varieties developed or selected through Cameroon’s agricultural research system.
The seed is multiplied under controlled conditions before being distributed to other farmers. Later generations gradually lose their genetic purity and performance, Mana said, and growers are advised not to continue planting the seed beyond the recommended cycle.
Seed multipliers must follow strict protocols. Their plots must be isolated to prevent varieties from mixing, while harvested seed cotton must remain separated during transport, storage and ginning. Facilities are cleaned before each seed lot is processed, and the cotton is labelled and stored by variety and batch.
Sarki uses a simple field test to judge the crop’s prospects. “When I break open a boll and find about eight or nine seeds, I know the harvest is going to be good,” he said.
According to Djallo, the cotton varieties grown by SODECOTON are IRMA Q302, IRMA A2188, IRMA Z2347, and IRMA D2A39, which are also displayed on the cotton production company's website.
Sarki said he has seen differences in how seed lines perform during dry periods, although variety, seed generation and growing conditions all influence the final yield.
“Even if there is no rain for about a week, when the farm is well cared for and kept free of insects, the harvest can still be good,” he said.
Improved seed is only one part of the effort to make cotton production more resilient. Farmers are also using agroecological practices that protect soil, retain water and make better use of organic matter already available on their farms.
At Gashiga Foulbe, Haman Bello grows the Q302 variety on 4.5 hectares inherited from his parents. He said he harvests about two tonnes per hectare. Mature Faidherbia albida trees growing among the cotton help enrich the soil and provide favourable conditions for the crop.
Unlike many trees, Faidherbia sheds its leaves during the rainy growing season. The fallen leaves add organic matter to the soil while the open canopy allows sunlight to reach the crop. The tree regains its leaves in the dry season, providing shade and fodder.
“Close to this tree, production is different and better,” Bello said.
He has also laid out ridges and planting rows across the slope rather than downhill, following advice from field technicians. The contour layout slows runoff and gives water more time to soak into the soil.
“When the slope is cut across, the crops retain water, which infiltrates deeply into the soil within a day or two and keeps the moisture,” Bello said. “Even when there is no rain, my plot retains water and the cotton grows normally. It is one way to respond to climate change.”
Other conservation methods promoted in the cotton belt include reducing tillage and leaving crop residue or straw on the soil. The cover limits erosion and water loss and, as it decomposes, adds organic matter. These practices can reduce — although not necessarily eliminate — farmers’ dependence on mineral fertiliser.
Boris Herman Talla, an agronomist, described agroecology as farming that protects soil, water and biodiversity while helping growers adapt to a changing climate.
“Agroecology can reduce farmers’ reliance on fertilisers, improve soil quality and strengthen resilience to climate change,” Talla said. He added that verified production methods may also help cotton reach specialised markets, although access to those markets and any price premium would need to be established.
The gains in the field do not automatically translate into comfortable incomes. Farmers said the producer price they receive has not kept pace with the cost of seed, fertiliser and crop protection products. Inputs are supplied on credit through producer organisations and the cost is deducted when the cotton is sold.
Researchers examining seventy years of cotton varietal improvement in Cameroon noted in 2019 that a number of cotton types had been successfully exported to other African nations, demonstrating the effectiveness and competitiveness of their varietal improvement programme.
SODECOTON has reported that in areas planted, cotton yield increased more than four-fold, confirming the farmers' experiences. Also, the production of cotton seed rose by 13.5%. Cameroonian cotton production is primarily in the long-fibre category, and the average agricultural yield has increased by 3.5 per cent, the company writes.
Mohammed Moussa, 46, has grown cotton for 28 years. He said he harvested 34 tonnes from 20 hectares last season — about 1.7 tonnes per hectare. The yield was substantial, but income still depended on the price paid and the cost of producing the crop.
Saki’s experience points to both the promise and the limits of Cameroon’s evolving cotton system. Better seed and farming methods can improve yields and protect the land, but their value to growers will ultimately be measured by how much income remains after the harvest is sold and the input loans are repaid.
For Sarki, cotton remains the household’s financial foundation.
“We do everything with the money from cotton,” he said. “We build houses, pay school fees, clothe the family and, if there is anything left, buy goats and sheep that we can sell to prepare for the next season.”

title: E-commerce digitalization for sustainable agricultural and rural development: models and pathways
content: This study adopts the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework as its core meso-level integrated explanatory framework, embedding digital empowerment theory to guide variable selection and causal logic. Meanwhile, it classifies the core conditional variables into technological capabilities, organizational capabilities, and environmental/structural factors, avoiding the stacking of practical dimensions in variable selection. We find that sustainable agricultural and rural development (SARD) outcomes are not driven by single factors but by the synergistic effect of multiple configurations. Analysis identifies three distinct pathways: digital technology and agile response-driven, service and channel optimization, and comprehensive synergy. The most effective pathway synergistically combines high channel integration, high digitalization of service experience, high marketing response agility, and high precision in consumer insight. These pathways enhance agricultural marketing efficiency and advance SARD across economic, social, and environmental dimensions. Furthermore, substitution effects exist among some auxiliary factors; for instance, depth of digital technology application and precision of consumer insight can be functionally equivalent in the digital technology and agile response-driven pathway. The core theoretical contribution of this study is breaking through the traditional linear cognition of single-factor driving in the research of digital agriculture and SARD, which is prevalent in both domestic and international academia. By adopting the fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) method, we identify and theorize three typical configurational driving archetypes of e-commerce-driven SARD, namely Technology-Agile type, Service-Optimized type and Comprehensive Synergy type, reveal the mechanisms of multiple concurrent causality and equifinal paths in the digital empowerment of SARD, supplement the configurational analysis perspective for the digital empowerment theory, and provide micro-practical support for the sustainable transition theory in the context of global digital agriculture and platformization development. We recommend that agricultural enterprises strengthen digital technology, build distinctive product identities based on consumer insights, and enhance service experiences to foster sustainable transitions.

title: Scientists spend another summer tagging sharks in Boston Harbor
content:
Support WBUR
Scientists spend another summer tagging sharks in Boston Harbor
Ryan Knotek stopped his boat and dropped anchor about a third of a mile off of Wollaston Beach. If he had the time, he could drink in the quintessentially Boston view: The skyline to the north, an outcropping of rocks where the chief of the Massachusett tribe used to hold meetings in front of him, one of Quincy’s Dunkin' Donuts closer to shore.
But Knotek, a New England Aquarium researcher, was too busy to admire the sights. He was there to catch some sharks.
Once upon a time Boston Harbor was one of the dirtiest ports in America. But decades of cleanup have turned it into an ecological haven for species like the sand tiger shark. By catching and tagging the generally placid fish, scientists hope to understand why they’re here, where they go, and what it means for them with a rapidly warming North Atlantic.
Knotek and his colleague, Emily Jones, are both with the aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life. They spend a lot of time in this inlet because young sand tiger sharks spend their summers there too.
“It's nice and sheltered, there aren't big sharks,” Jones said. “So it's, like, a safe place where they know they're going to find prey.”
Their team has tagged and tracked juvenile sand tiger sharks in Boston Harbor for almost a decade. Their research shows the same sharks come back year after year as the weather warms.
“You have this harbor that was at one point considered one of the dirtiest harbors in the U.S., and now these sharks are choosing to use this harbor for their summertime nursery ground,” Knotek said.
It’s a remarkable comeback story for a species that was once chronically overfished, with their population dropping by more than 70% along the East Coast, according to Knotek. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists sand tiger sharks as critically endangered on a global scale.
Federal and state regulations banned the fishing of these animals, starting in the late ‘90s.
“For the better part of two decades, they've had these protections, and we're starting to see recovery in their numbers,” Knotek said.
Each trip, the team baits their rods with frozen pogies and casts them out in hopes of catching a shark. Pogies are a favorite food for sand tiger sharks.
This bait is usually enough to land one, but if not, the team puts on music for luck. Knotek says their current list of favorites are Jimmy Buffet, the K-Pop Demon Hunters soundtrack and anything by Taylor Swift.
“They’re absolutely Swifties, fun fact,” Knotek said.
Once a shark is hooked, they bring it on deck, put it in a cooler and flip it on his back. That puts the shark into a sort of trance, called tonic immobility. The scientists then make a small incision in its belly and insert an acoustic transmitter, which allows the team to track the sharks they tag.
“So the same idea as your E-ZPass transponder in your car, and as soon as they swim by one of these receivers, the receiver detects that ping, it records which animal was there and what time it was,” he said.
Since 2023, the project has tagged about two dozen sharks, including four new juveniles this year. The New England Aquarium monitors about a dozen receivers in the harbor that track the sharks. All that data helps scientists figure out the best ways to support the sharks.
On a recent trip, Knotek analyzed data from two receivers in the Bay. They showed some familiar faces were still hanging around.
“So that shark that we also tagged last year on Sept. 5 has also been right over here within, like, the last half hour,” Knotek said. “So the shark's moving around a little bit, but they are here.”
Some researchers up and down the East Coast use the same tech, which allows them to share data about the sharks’ habits. It also lets them share information about threats, be it from fishing, habitat loss or climate change. The International Union for Conservation of Nature estimates a third of shark species globally are at risk for extinction.
With ocean water warming due to climate change, we may see more of them in the coming decades.. The sharks can’t regulate their own body temperature, so they depend on just-right water to warm and cool themselves. That means moving to different regions, depending on the season. Because temperatures in the North Atlantic are some of the highest ever recorded, sharks are seemingly traveling farther north than they had before.
Sharks, even juveniles like these sand tigers, are at the top of their food chain, according to Jones. Their health is an important marker for the rest of the ocean.
“It’s like the canary in the coal mine," Jones said. “If the sharks aren't doing well, something underneath them is broken. So they can be a really good indicator species, which makes them powerful to study.”

title: The Harvest Behind the Hard Currency: Ethiopia’s Agricultural Shift from Import Bills to Export Power
content:
The Harvest Behind the Hard Currency: Ethiopia’s Agricultural Shift from Import Bills to Export Power
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — A tonne of wheat grown at home can mean more than food in a national silo. It can mean foreign currency retained, pressure eased on the import bill and a little more room for a country to finance its own priorities.
A tonne of coffee exported can bring in the hard currency needed to pay for machinery, fuel, medicine and the technologies that domestic production still requires.
This is the economic story increasingly taking shape in Ethiopian agriculture: the sector is being repositioned not only as a source of food and rural livelihoods, but also as an instrument of foreign-exchange conservation, export expansion and wider economic transformation.
For years, wheat imports represented a substantial recurring demand on Ethiopia’s foreign currency. The Ministry of Agriculture says the country had been spending as much as one billion US dollars annually on wheat imports.
The expansion of domestic production across rainy and dry seasons has since sharply altered that picture. In 2025, Ethiopia produced a reported 280 million quintals of wheat, while the ministry estimated that domestic output had replaced 2.6 million quintals of imports and saved an average of one billion dollars annually.
The significance lies in the change to the country’s economic arithmetic. When a staple can be supplied increasingly from domestic farms, foreign exchange that would otherwise have gone toward imports can be retained for other national needs.
The gain is not automatic or unlimited: import requirements depend on domestic demand, harvest performance, prices and market conditions.
But the direction of the policy is clear—expand local productive capacity and reduce the structural cost of relying on overseas supply.
Wheat is only one side of that equation. Export agriculture provides the other.
Coffee, Ethiopia’s signature agricultural export, has become a major source of foreign currency. In the 2024/25 fiscal year, the country exported more than 470,000 tonnes of coffee and earned approximately 2.65 billion dollars.
In July 2026, the government announced that coffee export earnings had reached a new record of three billion dollars in the current fiscal year.
The coffee sector also illustrates how the value captured from agriculture depends on more than the size of the harvest. Quality improvements, productivity, direct export opportunities for farmers and access to international markets all influence how much value reaches producers and the national economy.
Ethiopia’s efforts to expand value-added coffee exports reflect a further ambition: to capture a larger share of the value generated beyond the farm gate, rather than relying predominantly on exports of raw beans.
Agriculture’s broader expansion adds depth to this shift. Ethiopia’s Government Communication Service reports that total agricultural output rose from 41.7 million tonnes to around 150 million tonnes over seven years, while cluster farming expanded to 9.5 million farmers cultivating 12.8 million hectares. Such growth enlarges the potential supply base for domestic markets, agro-processing and export-oriented production.
The strategic opportunity is to connect these gains into a functioning economic chain: higher productivity reduces import dependence; reliable surpluses create export opportunities; stronger value chains raise earnings; and domestic processing can retain more value within the country.
That chain requires investment in storage, transport, quality control, finance, processing and market access.
Production alone cannot guarantee foreign-exchange gains if the supporting systems remain weak.
Nor does agricultural expansion mean Ethiopia has outgrown its food-security challenges. The country continues to face vulnerability to climate shocks, conflict-related disruptions and market pressures. The USDA’s 2025 outlook, for example, projected that wheat imports would remain significant in the 2025/26 marketing year despite increased domestic production.
That distinction matters. Ethiopia’s agricultural transformation is not a declaration that imports or food insecurity have disappeared. It is a drive to reduce exposure, expand domestic supply and improve the country’s ability to earn foreign exchange from what its land and farmers produce.
The deeper change is in agriculture’s place within the national economy. Fields are increasingly connected to the balance of payments; harvests to industrial inputs; export crops to foreign-currency earnings; and food production to the country’s wider economic autonomy.
For Ethiopia, the harvest is becoming more than a measure of what the country can eat or sell. It is increasingly part of how the country finances what it wants to build.

title: Comparative efficacy of intra-articular polynucleotide injection combined with rehabilitation therapy in knee osteoarthritis with and without diabetes mellitus and construction of a nomogram: a propensity score-matched cohort study
content: ObjectiveTo compare the longitudinal clinical efficacy of intra-articular polynucleotide (PN) injection combined with prescribed rehabilitation therapy in patients with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), to investigate the influence of glycemic control on treatment outcomes, and to construct a predictive model.MethodsA total of 458 patients with KOA who received PN combined with rehabilitation therapy were retrospectively enrolled. After 1:2 propensity score matching (PSM), 270 patients were included (90 in the diabetes mellitus [DM] group and 180 in the non-DM group). Generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used to compare the longitudinal trajectories of Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores between the two groups. Stratified analyses were further performed within the DM subgroup according to baseline glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression combined with multivariable Logistic regression was used to construct a nomogram predicting the probability of achieving Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) at 6 months.ResultsAfter matching, no significant differences were observed between the two groups in the improvement trajectories of VAS and WOMAC scores (group effect, P > 0.05). Within the DM subgroup, the PASS achievement rate was significantly higher in patients with HbA1c < 7.0% than in those with HbA1c ≥ 7.0% (75.00% vs. 52.38%, P = 0.0248). The nomogram identified rehabilitation adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.95, 95% CI: 1.62–5.40), whereas uncontrolled DM (HbA1c ≥ 7.0%; OR = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.22–0.78), KL grade IV (OR = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.18–0.70), and BMI ≥ 28 kg/m2 (OR = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.35–0.96) were inversely associated with PASS achievement. The nomogram yielded a C-index of 0.82.ConclusionAmong patients with KOA receiving intra-articular PN injection together with a prescribed rehabilitation program, those with T2DM showed 6-month clinical outcome trajectories comparable to those without DM. Good glycemic control and favorable rehabilitation adherence are key factors for optimizing therapeutic outcomes.

title: Case Report: Streptococcus suis-associated meningoencephalitis with profound bilateral labyrinthine deafness and intra-operative cochlear fibrosis treated by cochlear implantation
content: Streptococcus suis is a common zoonotic pathogen that usually causes monomicrobial meningitis. Occult bloodstream detection of Klebsiella pneumoniae, together with proven central-nervous-system S. suis infection, followed by irreversible cochlear fibrotic changes requiring cochlear implantation, appears exceptionally rare. We report a 52-year-old male with chronic heavy alcohol intake and occupational swine-exposure history who developed severe sepsis, recurrent suppurative meningoencephalitis caused by S. suis, and permanent bilateral labyrinthine-related deafness. Combined blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) identified suspected additional bloodstream infection by K. pneumoniae, although K. pneumoniae was not detected in CSF. Multimodal antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapy cleared intracranial infection but failed to restore hearing. Preoperative imaging suggested cochlear fibrotic changes; left-sided cochlear implantation achieved full electrode insertion with stable intraoperative neural responses despite abundant intracochlear fibrous tissue observed intraoperatively. This case raises three important considerations: occupational swine exposure together with chronic alcoholism may plausibly contribute to suspected polymicrobial sepsis; in selected patients, peripheral-blood mNGS may help identify occult Gram-negative bacteremia when CSF assays remain negative during recurrent meningitis; and cochlear fibrosis may not absolutely preclude technically-successful cochlear implantation.

title: Ispostavilo se da je ova pasmina pasa zapravo dijelom - kojot
content:
Čivave su doista neobični psi. Volimo ih, ali nema sumnje da u tim malim stvorenjima ima nečeg pomalo… osebujnog.
Oglas
Novo istraživanje genetskog podrijetla pasa, objavljeno u časopisu Nature Communications, moglo bi donekle objasniti zašto. Ispostavilo se da čivave dijele dio gena s divljim kojotima (Canis latrans).
DNK – genetski nacrt zapisan u svakoj stanici tijela živog organizma – u sebi nosi povijest evolucije. Roditelji prenose svoj DNK potomstvu, a iako mutacije katkad mogu malo izmijeniti taj nacrt, upravo DNK omogućuje znanstvenicima da prate podrijetlo organizama kroz vrijeme, piše Science Alert.
Tu povijest nije lako iščitati, ali suvremena računalna tehnologija pomaže znanstvenicima dešifrirati tu golemu genetsku bazu podataka i bolje je razumjeti.
Tim sa Sveučilišta Stanford testirao je dva nova računalna programa, nazvana Gnomix i Gnofix, koji istodobno analiziraju genome velikog broja životinja i procjenjuju njihove međusobne srodstvene veze, rekonstruirajući tako njihovu evolucijsku povijest.
Taj postupak – stručno nazvan određivanje lokalnog podrijetla (local ancestry inference, LAI) – istraživačima može pomoći utvrditi podrijetlo pojedinih dijelova DNK unutar životinjskog genoma.
Upravo su tako naišli na poprilično neobičnu značajku u genomu najmanjeg psa na svijetu. Otkrili su da čivave s divljim kojotima dijele više segmenata svojeg genoma.
Već su postojali dokazi da su poznate suvremene meksičke pasmine – čivava i bezdlaki xoloitzcuintli, često nazivan jednostavno xolo – mješavina europskih i pretkolumbovskih pasa.
Većina današnjih pasmina domaćih pasa europskog je podrijetla, no te su dvije pasmine uspjele sačuvati dijelove svojeg podrijetla iz „Novog svijeta“.
Program Gnomix pomogao je potvrditi sjevernoameričko podrijetlo čivave i xola: u obiteljskom stablu čivave pronađeni su geni kojota, dok više od četiri posto genoma xola potječe od arktičkih pasa.
Studija nije otkrila kada su točno geni kojota mogli ući u genetsku lozu čivava, no prethodna istraživanja upućuju na to da se to dogodilo prije Kolumbova dolaska u Ameriku.
Također ne znamo je li križanje bilo namjerno ili slučajno niti koje su osobine čivave možda naslijedile od svojih autohtonih predaka – premda njihove goleme uši i izražajno zavijanje neodoljivo podsjećaju na kojote.
Za razliku od nekih drugih malih pasa za društvo, čivave su unatoč svojoj veličini poznate po neovisnom, ponosnom i samouvjerenom karakteru. Voljeli bismo vjerovati da je za to zaslužan divlji kojot koji se krije u njima, iako je to teško sa sigurnošću tvrditi.
„Utvrđeno je da se divlji kojoti i vukovi prirodno križaju, osobito na geografskim područjima na kojima su ponašajne osobine nalik vučjima korisne“, objasnila je zoologinja Jacqueline Boyd, koja nije sudjelovala u istraživanju, u članku za The Conversation.

title: Opinion: Social media bans are passing around the world. How will we know if they help teens?
content:
In December 2025, as social media’s potential impact on youth mental health faced growing scrutiny, Australia became the first country to ban social media for people under 16, with Indonesia quickly following. The European Union is taking a slightly different approach, banning social media for children under 13 and personal accounts for people under 15 after pressure from several E.U. nations.
Elsewhere, big tech companies are being challenged in the courts. Meta recently agreed to pay up to $18 billion to resolve claims in the U.S. that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. Meta will also introduce “safety by design” features for young people, such as concealing the number of “likes” on posts. But will these features meaningfully change young people’s behavior or experiences online? Will the bans have their intended effect?
With major changes being introduced around the world, researchers must seize this opportunity to conduct robust independent evaluations of how social media — and its regulation — impacts teenagers’ mental health, wellbeing and social lives. With almost half of all mental health problems emerging by the age of 18, this research is crucial.
One size might not fit all
Ultimately, the question is not simply whether social media is inherently “good” or “bad,” or whether restrictions “work” or “don’t work.” Instead, researchers need to look at whether changing young people’s digital environments leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing.
The evidence increasingly suggests that there is unlikely to be a single “social media effect” that impacts all teenagers in the same way.
Social media restrictions will likely affect individual young people differently, based on factors such as their age, whether they have existing mental health problems, and their sleep patterns. It could have different effects based on teenagers’ gender, their socioeconomic background, or where they live (for example, whether they come from an urban or rural area).
Social media can be an important source of community, so restrictions may affect people from marginalized backgrounds in different ways, including those who identify as LGBTQ+. It will most likely also depend on the specific way that a person uses (or previously used) a given platform.
If restrictions do bring changes in teenagers’ mental health, researchers need to understand the mechanisms behind the change. For example, if some young people experience an improvement in their mental health following the restrictions, might it be because they are meeting up more with friends in real life, or are they getting more sleep? The answer to the why question could shape future policies that support youth mental health.
Lessons from Australia
Early findings from Australia suggest that age verification from social media companies is a significant challenge in implementing the ban.
An evaluation published in the British Medical Journal found little evidence of substantial reductions in social media use three months after Australia implemented its ban. It found that many young people were continuing to use restricted platforms and finding ways around age-verification systems. Meanwhile, a report by Australia’s online watchdog found that more than 80% of children were still using a restricted online platform.
Behavioral economist Leonardo Bursztyn and colleagues found that many teenagers continued to believe their peers were using restricted platforms and reported they would be more willing to stop if more of their peers stopped, too. This shows the importance of peer influence in adolescent decision-making, which will be a factor in the restrictions globally.
The difficulties in implementing the ban in Australia mean that it is still too early to say whether it has improved young people’s mental health and in what ways it has worked. Still, this raises an important point that implementation will be a major factor across the world.
Assessing the change in the U.K.
In the U.K., the government is planning to introduce a social media ban in spring 2027.
I work at Wellcome, a global philanthropic foundation based in London and one of the biggest funders of mental health research in the world. We are going to be funding evaluations of the impact of the social media ban in the U.K. on youth mental health, with research teams working with tens of thousands of teenagers. All our work is guided by young people with experience in both social media use and mental health problems, so that research best reflects their concerns.
In this case, we consulted with a group of young people to ask for advice on how best to design and implement the research on social media restrictions. The young people reframed the whole debate. Rather than focusing solely on whether social media is harmful and whether we need a ban, they repeatedly asked us to look at what role social media currently plays in young people’s lives — and what might replace it if access is restricted.
Young people are not oblivious about the risks of social media, such as misinformation and harmful content, but they also recognize it as infrastructure for learning, connection, support, creativity, and belonging. They highlighted that evaluating the restrictions requires understanding how teenagers’ time is otherwise spent. For example, they said, researchers should look at whether young people are spending time in a positive way by cultivating outdoor hobbies, friendships, sleeping better, and studying more. Or will they simply spend the time being bored, or find themselves in unregulated online spaces?
In short, the young people were asking researchers to evaluate changes in their lives, rather than simply looking at changes in their screen time.
They suggested that the evaluation should not only focus on how to reduce harm, but also on understanding what kinds of social environments best support young people’s mental health and wellbeing.
A global opportunity
We are not simply trying to evaluate the U.K. government’s policy on banning social media. We are trying to understand a much broader and fundamental question: How do changes in the digital environment impact young people’s mental health and wellbeing, and why?
While we are focusing on the U.K., this is a globally relevant question. Comparing what happens in Australia and the U.K., with the results in the E.U., where they will be cracking down on certain practices, and elsewhere in the world, via Meta’s new tools, will be illuminating. Perhaps we will end up learning that bans are the solution. Perhaps some tools will be more effective than others.
There is a seismic opportunity for research teams around the world to join forces to evaluate how social media and its restrictions impact youth mental health. The answers that emerge could influence how we intervene in youth mental health for generations to come.
Camilla Iannone is research lead in the mental health evidence team at Wellcome.

title: Tiny wallaby spotted on Australia trail cameras for the first time in 50 years: 'Great news for the species'
content:
Researchers at the Australian Wildlife Conservancy are rejoicing after a major discovery: Confirmed sightings of a tiny wallaby for the first time in 50 years.
The Nabarlek is Australia’s second-smallest wallaby, and new trail camera footage confirmed its presence at two new locations in Western Australia’s Kimberley region.
The camera traps — and a scat analysis — verified the presence of the 2.6-pound (or 1.2-kilogram) rock-wallaby on Yampi Sound Training Area on Dambeemangaddee Country. A second population was also confirmed around 105 miles away in the northeast of Dambeemangaddee Country.
These were the first detections of the species on mainland Dambeemangaddee Country in over 50 years, and the first on record for the Yampi Sound Training Area, one of 20 priority places for the federal government’s “threatened species action plan.”
Seeing these tiny wallabies in the wild provides both major insight into the species’ ecology and hope for the endangered species in the northern part of the country.
“This is very exciting and great news for the species,” Larissa Potter, AWC senior field ecologist, said.
“Confirming the Nabarlek’s presence at two new sites on mainland Dambeemangaddee Country is a major step forward for our understanding of where the species occurs. It’s also reassuring as it indicates that this threatened wallaby is persisting on the Kimberley mainland in places we didn’t previously know about.”
The Nabralek is believed to have once been widespread across the area, but in recent years, there have been very few records of the species in any part of Australia. Feral cats, more herbivores influencing the ecosystem, and severe wildfires may be to blame for the species’ decline.
About as long as a loaf of bread, the tiny critters are also elusive, due to the fact that they live in very remote, rocky habitats.
Additionally, the Nabralek looks very similar to two other wallaby species, the Monjon and the Short-eared Rock-wallaby, making it even harder for researchers to confirm the species’ presence.
The AWC worked with the Dambimangari Aboriginal Corporation to study the Nabralek, using camera images and genetic analysis through scat samples, later examining the images more thoroughly for distinctive markings and physical traits that differentiate the species from other wallabies.
“Every animal has its own song and story, they might be small, they might be big, but they all play their part in keeping [the country] healthy. They’re part of the ecosystem,” Inga Pedersen, Dambeemangaddee traditional owner, said.
“We heard that the Nabarlek didn't exist anymore [on the mainland], so it’s good to know that they’re there; it shows their country is healthy.”
Now, the AWC and DAC will continue to survey the area to find more Nabarlek populations. This will allow them to further investigate threats facing the species and implement conservation efforts to protect it.
“Now we want to know more about them. Is it a healthy population?” Pederson said. “We want to compare them to the ones on the islands, and make sure this animal isn't disappearing.”
