title: Plans to turn Rugezi Wetland into national park gain momentum
content: Plans to turn Rugezi Wetland and the surrounding areas into Rwanda’s fifth national park are gaining momentum, with a study on the proposed project expected to be completed by December 2026, Northern Province Governor Maurice Mugabowagahunde has said. The proposed Rugezi, Burera and Ruhondo National Park would bring together the wetland and the islands of Lakes Burera and Ruhondo, creating a new ecotourism destination while strengthening biodiversity conservation. Rugezi Wetland covers approximately 6,735 hectares across Burera and Gicumbi districts. Located at an altitude of about 2,100 metres, it is an important source of water flowing towards the Nile River and supplies water used by the Ntaruka hydropower plant. ALSO READ: Rugezi wetland records surge in grey-crowned crane population “Studies for a project to turn Rugezi Wetland into Rwanda’s fifth national park are at an advanced stage, with the study expected to be completed by December 2026,” Mugabowagahunde said. The governor made the remarks during the inauguration of Rugezi Community Centre in Ibanda Cell, Miyove Sector, Gicumbi District, near the wetland. He said the first phase of research had identified wildlife attractions beyond the grey crowned cranes for which Rugezi is widely known. “The first part of the research, which looked at what visitors to Rugezi Wetland could see, has been completed, and we found that, besides the grey crowned cranes, there are other species of wildlife that people did not know were there,” he said. The next phase, involving a scientific study, is already under way and is expected to be completed in December. The project also envisages improving road access to the wetland, extending electricity to residents who currently rely on solar power, and developing hotel facilities to accommodate visitors. ALSO READ: How Rugezi wetland restoration stabilised hydropower supply Mugabowagahunde said the planned park would help showcase other tourism attractions in Northern Province beyond mountain gorillas. Over 30 experts conducting studies The Rwanda Development Board (RDB) has announced that more than 30 experts from different countries have begun studying the establishment of the proposed Rugezi, Burera and Ruhondo National Park and a separate Kivu Islands National Park. The experts specialise in biodiversity, business, economics and community livelihoods. They are working with representatives from RDB, the Rwanda Environment Management Authority, Rwanda Forestry Authority, Water and Sanitation Corporation, and Rwanda Water Resources Board while RWCA is conducting feasibility study. The proposed Rugezi park would combine the wetland’s biodiversity with the scenic landscapes and islands of Lakes Burera and Ruhondo. Lake Burera alone has nine islands. The establishment of the proposed park could cost more than Rwf3 billion. A recent biodiversity survey conducted by the Rwanda Wildlife Conservation Association (RWCA) identified 741 species in Rugezi Wetland, including 472 that had not previously been recorded there. The survey documented 197 plant species, 134 bird species and 53 mammal species, including 22 bat species. ALSO READ: Rugezi wetland: Crane habitat under threat from grass-cutting Rugezi is also an important habitat for the grey crowned crane, which is classified as Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. According to RWCA data, the number of grey crowned cranes recorded in the wetland increased from 71 in 2017 to 378 in 2026. BirdLife International has also classified Rugezi as an Important Bird Area because it supports threatened bird species, including the grey crowned crane and Bradypterus graueri, a songbird species. The proposed park is expected to strengthen protection of these species and other wildlife found in the wetland and on the islands of Lakes Burera and Ruhondo. New community centre to support conservation The Rwf269 million Rugezi Community Centre, constructed by RWCA, is intended to provide alternative livelihoods for residents living near the wetland, particularly women involved in tailoring and weaving. The facility currently accommodates 45 women, many of whom previously engaged in activities prohibited in the wetland, including grass-cutting, due to limited income opportunities. It provides free working space and sewing machines, enabling the women to produce and sell their products to visitors and travellers. ALSO READ: Govt probes wildfire on 7,000 ha Rugezi wetland The centre also has a coffee shop where visitors can purchase refreshments and locally made handicrafts. Mugabowagahunde said the facility demonstrates how environmental conservation can directly benefit surrounding communities. He noted that providing women with a suitable working environment and access to potential customers would help them earn a living while reducing pressure on the wetland. RWCA Director-General Dr Olivier Nsengimana said the centre was established to improve community welfare through alternative livelihoods that support environmental conservation. He said such initiatives also help protect the wetland by reducing activities that contribute to environmental degradation and soil erosion. Women welcome new opportunities Yvette Uzarama, president of Miyove Sewing Women Cooperative, said the new facility would allow members to work without the disruptions they previously experienced. The cooperative, which has 30 members from Miyove and Nyankenke sectors, formerly operated from a building temporarily provided by the district. Its activities were sometimes interrupted when the building was needed for meetings or other purposes. “Here, we will be able to work every day and at any time we want, unless there is no one at the facility,” Uzarama said. Established by women who began working together after completing their studies in 2024, the cooperative initially relied on small orders but has gradually expanded, with RWCA helping members access markets. ALSO READ: Rugezi water tower on the rise Uzarama said the cooperative has accumulated approximately Rwf1.5 million in savings, while its equipment brings the estimated value of its assets to about Rwf2.2 million. “Our goal is to keep working and developing ourselves while avoiding activities that damage Rugezi Marsh,” she said. Elina Rukundo, president of Dukunde Umurimo Twiteze Imbere Rugezi Cooperative, said its 14 members previously worked individually from their homes before joining forces. The cooperative produces woven decorations and other handicrafts, which RWCA helps market. Rukundo said conservation awareness had changed how residents viewed the wetland, where some previously harvested grass, grazed livestock, hunted grey crowned cranes and collected their eggs. “I cannot go there to destroy it today because I have learned that Rugezi Marsh is home to different species and is important to us,” she said. She added that the growing tourism potential of Rugezi presents opportunities for surrounding communities to earn income while contributing to the protection of the wetland.

title: Liberia: Liberia Targets $30b Natural Capital Through Carbon Market
content:
Liberia has unveiled an ambitious vision to transform more than $30 billion in estimated natural capital--including forests, mangroves, biodiversity and renewable-energy potential--into a foundation for sustainable economic growth, climate resilience and peace.
The initiative was placed at the center of Liberia's engagement at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, where the government convened a high-level discussion on the links between climate change, natural resources, conflict and sustainable development.
Organized by Liberia's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the event brought together senior Liberian officials and international climate and development experts to examine how natural resources can become engines of inclusive development rather than sources of conflict.
For Liberia, the centerpiece was the emerging natural-capital strategy being advanced under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, with Presidential Envoy on Climate Action and Chief Executive Officer of the Liberian Carbon Market Authority, Hon. Janine Cooper, outlining efforts to measure, value and monetize environmental assets while ensuring communities benefit.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
Cooper said Liberia's natural abundance provides an economic opportunity extending far beyond traditional extraction of timber and minerals.
With more than 5,000 millimeters of annual rainfall, 15 rivers, extensive forests and biodiversity, significant sunshine and a 579-kilometer coastline, Liberia possesses natural assets that can support climate financing, sustainable agriculture, conservation, renewable energy and other emerging economic sectors.
Under the Boakai administration, Cooper said, Liberia is working to bring these resources under an integrated natural-capital framework estimated at more than $30 billion.
The initiative represents a shift in how Liberia presents its environmental assets--not simply as resources to be protected, but as measurable national wealth capable of generating investment, livelihoods and long-term development.
Weeks before the UNGA gathering, the Liberian Carbon Market Authority presented Liberia's first National Carbon Policy to President Boakai after approximately a year of work establishing digital infrastructure and valuation systems to determine the carbon value associated with specific land parcels.
Cooper said Liberia wants to position itself as a supplier of high-integrity, nature-based climate solutions, allowing the country to attract financing while maintaining the environmental integrity of its forests and ecosystems.
But she emphasized that natural capital must translate into tangible benefits for communities.
Her presentation linked the strategy directly to peacebuilding, arguing that environmental investments can prevent local conflicts even before carbon credits or other climate-financing instruments generate revenue.
Mangrove restoration, she explained, can reduce flooding and prevent families from being displaced to areas where competition for land could generate new disputes. Climate-smart agriculture can similarly improve productivity and reduce pressure on farmers to expand into neighboring community forests.
"Peace, in Liberia, is often local before it is national," Cooper said.
Opening the event, EPA Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo said Liberia's experience of peacebuilding provides an important foundation for addressing environmental pressures that could deepen social and economic tensions.
He warned that climate pressures can exacerbate existing vulnerabilities where institutions are weak and communities are excluded from decisions over natural resources.
Liberia's forests, minerals, rivers, fisheries and coastal ecosystems, he said, can drive national development if managed through strong governance systems and in ways that provide meaningful benefits to communities.
UNDP Associate Administrator Haoliang Xu argued that climate change, peace, development and natural-resource governance are increasingly inseparable.
Xu cited the World Meteorological Organization's confirmation that 2024 was the warmest year on record and said climate impacts are compounding pressures involving displacement, land access and unresolved grievances globally.
He highlighted Liberia's climate commitments, noting that the country contributes approximately 0.03 percent of global emissions but has committed under its NDC 3.0 to cutting economy-wide emissions by 64 percent by 2040, with adaptation targets covering seven sectors.
Xu also noted that peace and security considerations now feature in 41 percent of third-generation national climate plans globally, rising to 70 percent in fragile states.
"Climate change need not be a narrative of conflict and instability," Xu said. "With the right choices, climate action can strengthen livelihoods, improve natural resource governance, and sustain peace."
Kenya's Special Envoy on Climate Change, Ambassador Ali D. Mohamed, described how environmental pressures can contribute to competition over land and water.
With approximately 80 percent of Kenya classified as arid land, Mohamed said conflict between farmers and herders can intensify around rainfall, grazing areas and water availability.
He cited the Dadaab refugee complex, which has existed for more than three decades, as an example of how prolonged humanitarian crises can place sustained pressure on local resources and host communities.
He also highlighted Kigali's use of wetlands as flood-absorbing parks and Nairobi's urban forests as examples of environmental investments supporting resilience and development.
Rep. Naquetta Ricks, President of the African Chamber of Commerce and an advocate for Liberia through the Liberian Surfing Association, urged Liberia to broaden its forest economy.
With more than 40 percent of the country still covered by forests, Ricks said Liberia should move beyond conventional timber concessions and expand community-based activities such as agroforestry, ecotourism and carefully regulated carbon financing.
She also called for stronger oversight of mining and logging and greater community involvement in natural-resource decisions, while urging the Liberian diaspora to contribute technical expertise, investment and accountability.
Daniel Kennedy of Australia's Minderoo Foundation warned of intensifying global climate pressures and argued that nature's economic value must be placed at the center of development planning.
Echoing Minderoo founder Dr. Andrew Forrest's position that "nature is the real economy," Kennedy said philanthropic organizations could increasingly help address financing gaps as traditional development assistance declines, while acknowledging that philanthropy cannot replace government institutions.
For Liberia, the discussions come as the country prepares to assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.
The $30 billion natural-capital vision is therefore emerging as part of the Boakai administration's broader economic and diplomatic strategy to demonstrate that forests, biodiversity, carbon resources and other natural assets can become productive national wealth while supporting communities, climate resilience and peace.

title: Federated learning in a regulator-audited secure processing environment: a multi-hospital deployment study
content: Background. Federated learning enables collaborative model development without transferring patient level data between institutions. However, translation into routine healthcare practice remains limited because deployment requires more than distributed model training. Federated infrastructures must operate within secure processing environments, satisfy governance and security requirements, support auditability, and integrate with existing regulatory workflows for secondary use of health data. Although federated learning has been demonstrated in multiple clinical applications, evidence for its deployment, assessment, and operation within regulated health-data infrastructures remains limited. Methods. We implemented a decentralised swarm learning system for federated learning and integrated it into Acamedic, a certified secure processing environment (SPE) operated by Helsinki University Hospital (HUS). Introduction of the swarm learning coordination layer constituted a material modification to the previously certified HUS SPE and triggered a differential regulatory security assessment under Finland's Act on the Secondary Use of Health and Social Data and associated Findata requirements. The assessment evaluated controls relating to data isolation and locality, identity and access management, logging and monitoring, network security, and environment protection, while establishing a governance model that separates certification of infrastructure-level controls from study specific assessment of data, models, parameter exchanges, and outputs. The swarm learning architecture was developed and deployed across the university hospitals of Helsinki, Turku, and Tampere, with HUS serving as the regulator-assessed implementation within a certified SPE and partner sites operating under local institutional governance frameworks. As an operational exemplar, we trained federated DeepSurv survival models for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) using harmonised longitudinal laboratory data. Findings. The differential security assessment identified one high-severity, two medium-severity, and two low-severity findings. All high- and medium-severity findings were remediated and verified, after which an independent certification report was issued for the assessed extension. The resulting federated-learning capability was authorised for secondary use of health data and operationalised as a reusable extension to the HUS secure processing environment. Swarm learning was successfully executed across three university hospitals without transferring patient-level data, achieving 100% parameter merge success. Training operations were traceable through infrastructure logs, container logs, and a distributed ledger coordination layer recording participant registration, parameter exchanges, and model-training lineage. On independent test sets from all three hospitals, the swarm-trained AML model demonstrated stronger risk stratification than locally trained reference models, with consistently stronger risk separation, higher log-hazard ratios (swarm vs local: 4.32 vs 1.79 at HUS, 7.20 vs 3.19 at TAYS, and 5.90 vs 2.91 at TYKS), and improved discrimination metrics. The resulting federated-learning capability was authorised for secondary use of health data, operationalised as a reusable extension to the HUS secure processing environment, and made available for future permit approved analyses. Interpretation. This study demonstrates that federated learning can be integrated into a certified secure processing environment, subjected to regulatory assessment, and operated across independent hospitals without centralising patient level data. The principal contribution is a reusable governance and infrastructure model that separates assessment of system-level controls from study specific evaluation of data, models, parameter exchanges, and outputs. By enabling federated learning to function as an assessed infrastructure capability rather than a project-specific exception, the approach provides a practical pathway for operationalising decentralised federated learning within regulated health-data environments. The findings are directly relevant to emerging European frameworks for secondary use of health data, including secure processing environments envisioned under the European Health Data Space, whose implementation builds on many of the same governance principles evaluated in this study.

title: Azerbaijan MFA: Restoration of state sovereignty created new political reality in region

Happy State Sovereignty Day, Azerbaijan!"

title: WA’s Indigenous Desert Alliance ranger teams sole Australian nominees for Prince William’s Earthshot prize
content:
A group of WA based Indigenous rangers have been named the only Australian finalists for Prince William’s Earthshot Prize.
The Indigenous Desert Alliance – made up of a group of about 70 indigenous ranger teams – were picked from a field of almost 700 nominations.
Its Right Way Desert Fire program combines Indigenous knowledge with modern approaches to reduce bushfire risk.
The Indigenous ranger teams use carefully timed ground and aerial burning to create a mosaic of vegetation at different stages of recovery.
This improves habitats for native species, lowers fuel loads and reduces the risk of vast, uncontrolled fires.
Alliance chief executive Samantha Murray a Yilka, Wongutha and Nyoongar woman said becoming an Earthshot Prize finalist would bring greater visibility to the group.
“IDA exists to serve desert mob and the rangers caring for Country every day, connecting their work across the desert,” Ms Murray said.
“The next few years are crucial with the increased impacts of climate change and an uncertain funding future.
“Being selected as an Earthshot Prize Finalist gives us a stronger platform to show why right-way fire, threatened-species work and knowledge passed from Elders to younger people must be supported and funded for the long term.
“That means stronger ranger teams, healthy Country and decisions about the desert staying in Indigenous hands. Deserts thrive best when Indigenous people are leading.”
IDA is one of 15 nominees competing for one of five prizes of $1.9m (AUD).
Earthshot founder Prince William said every year the finalists give him renewed optimism.
“They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible,” he added.
“Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act.
“When they succeed, they inspire others and accelerate change.”
The winners will be announced in Mumbai in November.

title: Validation of the Gazelle point-of-care device for hemoglobin variant analysis in a predominantly pediatric population: performance comparison with conventional electrophoresis
content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of genetic hemoglobinopathies that lead to significant morbidity and mortality including vaso-occlusive crises, hemolysis, and progressive organ damage. Early detection is critical to initiate disease-modifying therapy and prevent complications; however, conventional hemoglobin electrophoresis is often unavailable in low-resource settings where SCD is most prevalent. Point-of-care (POC) devices offer a potential solution by enabling rapid, low-cost screening. The Gazelle POC instrument, which separates hemoglobin variants (A, F, S, and A2/CE) on a cellulose acetate membrane, has been evaluated in limited populations, but its performance relative to conventional electrophoresis methods in pediatric samples remains underexplored. This study validated the analytical and clinical performance of Gazelle using predominantly pediatric whole blood. Precision, linearity, and method comparison studies were conducted with quality control materials and 46 clinical samples analyzed on both Gazelle and the Sebia Capillarys system. Results showed variable precision across hemoglobin variants, strong linearity for Hb A (R2 ≥ 0.95), and high correlation (R2 > 0.95) for Hb A, F, and S. These findings support the potential use of Gazelle for SCD screening in children, particularly in resource-limited settings.

title: Crested Ibises Released to Help Restore Wild Range
content:
“Twenty crested ibises were released into the wild in Xiaolong Mountain, Tianshui city, Gansu province, on Sunday. This marks a new stage in the province's efforts to restore wild populations of the endangered bird, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
These crested ibises underwent strict rewilding training and health checks before being fitted with identification tags and released. The move is expected to help the species return to its historical distribution areas, expand its survival space in the wild, and improve the regional conservation network, the administration stated in a media release.
In 1981, only seven wild individuals of the bird were discovered in Yangxian county, Shaanxi province, believed to be the last of their kind. Thanks to over four decades of dedicated conservation, the global population of the crested ibis has now surpassed 10,000, with most residing in Yangxian.”

title: The human brain clears fluid directly into the skull, and poor sleep slows the process down
content:
Brain fluid drains directly into the spongy marrow of the human skull, establishing a physical connection between the nervous system and the immune system. A recent imaging study reveals that this drainage process is slower in older individuals and those experiencing poor sleep or cognitive decline. The research was published in the journal eLife.
Historically, biologists thought the central nervous system was entirely isolated from the rest of the body. A specialized cellular boundary called the blood-brain barrier supposedly prevented immune cells and other substances from entering or leaving the brain. This isolation was thought to protect delicate neural tissue from damaging inflammation. Recent discoveries have challenged this view of the nervous system, revealing that the brain communicates directly with the surrounding bone.
Studies in mice and human tissue have identified tiny physical channels connecting the brain’s outer protective layers directly to the bone marrow inside the skull. The bone marrow is a spongy tissue inside bones that produces blood cells and immune cells. These microscopic channels allow cerebrospinal fluid to exit the brain and interact with the immune cells residing in the skull. Cerebrospinal fluid is the colorless liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord, acting as a waste removal system for the nervous system.
To better understand how this fluid moves in living humans, researchers at Zhejiang University in China organized an imaging study. The research team, led by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, and Min Lou, wanted to map exactly where and how fast the fluid travels into the skull. They also wanted to see if medical conditions, sleep quality, and memory might relate to how well this fluid system functions.
The researchers enrolled 87 patients who were already scheduled to receive a spinal tap for various neurological conditions. The medical team injected a contrast agent called gadolinium into the cerebrospinal fluid in the lower back of each patient. Gadolinium shows up brightly on magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, allowing researchers to track the fluid as it travels up the spine and into the head.
The patients underwent MRI scans before the injection and at three later time points. These follow-up scans occurred at 4.5 hours, 15 hours, and 39 hours after the initial injection. The research team focused their analysis on the bone marrow in three specific areas of the skull. They looked at the top of the head near a major vein called the superior sagittal sinus, the sides of the skull near the lateral fissure, and the base of the skull near the cisterna magna.
To measure the concentration of the contrast agent, the researchers compared the signal in the skull marrow against a reference point in the eyeball. The fluid inside the eye does not absorb the contrast agent, providing a stable baseline. By calculating the ratio between the skull signal and the eye signal, the team could track how much fluid had reached the bone marrow at each time point.
To evaluate health and lifestyle factors, the researchers also administered questionnaires to the participants. They used a standard survey to assess sleep quality over the previous month, looking at factors like sleep duration and nighttime disturbances. One month after the patients left the hospital, researchers evaluated their cognitive performance using a telephone-based test that measures attention, language, memory, and orientation.
The MRI scans showed the contrast agent moving from the cerebrospinal fluid directly into the skull bone marrow. The speed of this fluid movement varied depending on the anatomical region. Fluid reached the bone marrow at the top of the head the fastest. For a majority of the patients, the contrast agent peaked in this top region at the 4.5-hour mark.
Fluid movement into the bone marrow at the base of the skull was much slower. In half of the patients, the contrast agent did not peak in this lower region until 15 hours after the injection. The researchers hypothesize that fluid might travel through alternative pathways between the skull and the brain, speeding up delivery to the top of the head while bypassing other areas.
The researchers then analyzed what biological factors might influence the speed of fluid drainage near the top of the head. They found that older age, high blood pressure, and diabetes all correlated with slower fluid movement into the skull bone marrow. Female patients also showed slower drainage compared to male patients.
The drainage patterns were also linked to signs of systemic inflammation. Patients with slower fluid drainage had higher percentages of neutrophils, but lower percentages of monocytes and lymphocytes, in their blood. Neutrophils and monocytes are types of white blood cells that respond to infections and injuries. This suggests that higher levels of inflammation in the body might restrict the flow of cerebrospinal fluid into the skull marrow.
The patient questionnaires revealed a link between fluid drainage, sleep, and memory. Patients who reported worse sleep quality had slower drainage into the skull bone marrow at the top of the head. Slower drainage also correlated with lower scores on the cognitive telephone test.
Through statistical analysis, the researchers explored whether this drainage system might bridge the known gap between poor sleep and memory problems. Their calculations showed that the speed of fluid drainage accounted for roughly 38 percent of the statistical association between poor sleep and lower cognitive scores. The research team proposed that sleep disturbances might worsen inflammation, which in turn slows down fluid drainage and contributes to cognitive decline.
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot prove that slow fluid drainage causes cognitive decline or sleep problems. The statistical links only show that these variables change in tandem. Additionally, the patients in the study all had existing neurological conditions, such as peripheral neuropathy or encephalitis. Without a comparison group of healthy individuals, it remains unknown if these fluid dynamics operate the same way in the general public.
The methods used to measure sleep and cognition also present limitations. The researchers relied on self-reported questionnaires and telephone interviews rather than objective physiological measurements. A clinical sleep study measuring brain waves would provide a more accurate picture of how specific sleep stages relate to fluid movement.
The interpretation of the imaging timeline requires caution. The researchers classified the highest MRI signal at 4.5 hours as an indicator of drainage efficiency. This early time frame might just represent the fluid entering the bone marrow, while the later scans might better reflect the fluid actually washing out of the tissue. Future imaging studies with more frequent scanning intervals will be required to map the exact timeline of fluid entering and exiting the skull.
The study, “Skull Bone Marrow Drainage and Its Associations with Inflammation, Sleep Quality, and Cognitive Performance,” was authored by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, Xiao Zhu, Yifei Li, Ziyu Zhou, Xin Huang, Huihong Ke, Mengmeng Fang, Jianzhong Sun, and Min Lou.

title: Municipal Leadership in Ocean Conservation Unites 500 Mayors Across Eight Countries
content:
A Filipino mayor’s coastal protection efforts inspired counterparts in Honduras, sparking a global network that proves municipal leadership in ocean conservation outperforms distant, top-down policy.
Before 2021, mayors in coastal towns across the Philippines had spent years defending fisheries their communities depended on, working with the international conservation organization Rare to protect nearshore waters. Their success traveled further than anyone anticipated, inspiring municipal leaders in Honduras to adopt similar approaches an ocean away.
That cross-border inspiration became formalized on World Oceans Day 2021, when 60 mayors pledged to protect coastal seas, launching what became Coastal 500. Municipal leadership in ocean conservation had found its structure: a global network connecting local government leaders directly with one another, bypassing the slow pace of national bureaucracy to share solutions that actually work on the water.
The premise driving this approach is straightforward. Roughly 200 million people worldwide depend directly or indirectly on coastal fisheries for their livelihoods. A narrow 12-kilometer band of ocean holds more than 70% of all marine biodiversity, yet only 10% of the world’s ocean and coastal areas are currently protected. Global financing for ocean health remains critically thin, with just 1% of sustainable development funding directed toward life below water.
Municipal leadership in ocean conservation fills a gap that national governments and international bodies often cannot. Mayors sit in a unique position between their communities and higher levels of government. Through local councils, community events, and everyday conversations, they understand fishing families’ daily struggles more intimately than any distant ministry could. When disasters strike, such as coastal flooding, drought, or powerful storms, it is mayors who coordinate emergency response and rally local resources first.
This proximity became evident when Typhoon Rai, locally named Odette, struck the Philippine municipality of Del Carmen in 2021. A decade of mangrove rehabilitation and preservation efforts, led locally rather than imposed from above, allowed the coastal community to withstand the four-hour super storm with minimal loss of life and property. Residents had spent years protecting them, and the mangroves ultimately protected them in return, offering both physical storm defense and a stable food source when it mattered most.
Momentum built steadily following the network’s 2021 launch. In March 2022, member mayors issued their first joint statement at the 8th Our Ocean Conference, marking the International Year of the Artisanal Fisher. By September 2023, municipal leadership in ocean conservation earned global recognition when Coastal 500 was selected from more than 1,300 nominees as a finalist for the prestigious Earthshot Prize.
The network’s reach expanded into major international forums throughout 2023 and beyond. Members participated in the COP28 Local Climate Action Summit in Dubai, then hosted their first global peer-learning exchange in the Philippines in June 2024, where local leaders shared strategies directly with one another and joined the National Coastal and Inland Fisheries Summit.
By 2025, municipal leadership in ocean conservation had formalized partnerships with major global alliances including Together for the Ocean, the Global Mangrove Alliance, and Revive Our Oceans, embedding the mayor-led network within broader international ocean protection efforts. That June, the largest Coastal 500 delegation yet engaged at the second United Nations Ocean Conference in France, coinciding with the launch of the Ocean Rise and Coastal Resilience Coalition.
Brazilian members brought previously underrepresented local perspectives to COP30 in November 2025, speaking directly at ministerial events and securing recognition of network commitments within the official COP30 Global Action Agenda. By March 2026, Coastal 500 surpassed its founding goal, reaching more than 500 active members across eight countries stewarding over 100,000 square kilometers of coastal waters.
Governor Henaro Polloi of Melekeok, Palau, described how local fishers and village chiefs have stewarded their ocean waters for generations, and how efforts to formalize and strengthen their fishing rights could serve as a blueprint for other island nations. In Honduras, Mayor Noel Ruiz of Santa Fe emphasized that mayors achieve far more collectively than individually, using shared experience to elevate the voices of artisanal fishers too often positioned at the bottom of national economic priorities.
Juan Ramón Manaiza, mayor of Limón, Honduras, credited the network directly with sparking his community’s coastal protection movement after learning from Philippine counterparts, framing the exchange as proof that collective action safeguards shared futures across vastly different coastlines and cultures.
Municipal leadership in ocean conservation operates through four coordinated strategies. Local action and policy support help members develop practical solutions responsive to their specific community needs. Global advocacy elevates local priorities onto international platforms, translating grassroots leadership into influence over policy and funding decisions typically reserved for national delegations. Peer-to-peer learning connects governments across regions, allowing proven approaches to spread organically rather than through top-down mandate. Capacity building strengthens members’ long-term ability to sustain impact well beyond any single mayoral term.
As climate change intensifies coastal flooding, warming waters, and shifting fish migrations, municipal leadership in ocean conservation offers something increasingly rare: trusted local messengers who can shape community norms and inspire sustainable practice from within, rather than imposing it from outside. What began with Filipino mayors sharing hard-won lessons with Honduran counterparts has become a structural model for how coastal protection might actually scale, one municipality, one mayor, and one community at a time.

title: 멸종위기 Ⅱ급 ‘큰바늘꽃’ 이식 개체 현지 적응 성공 확인
content:
청송군 주방천 큰바늘꽃 이식지에서 지난 1년간 자연 번식으로 개체수 2.5배 증가
기후에너지환경부 산하 국립생태원은 경상북도 청송군 주방천 일대에 이식한 멸종위기 야생생물 Ⅱ급인 큰바늘꽃 개체가 현지 적응에 성공한 것을 최근 확인했다고 밝혔다.
큰바늘꽃은 경상북도, 강원도, 울릉도의 하천과 계곡 주변 자갈밭이나 축축한 모래땅에 무리 지어 살던 여러해살이풀이다. 하천의 생물다양성을 구성하는 중요한 종이지만, 무분별한 하천 개발로 대부분의 원자생지가 훼손되어 개체군이 감소했다.
줄기 높이 1~2m까지 자라며 잎은 서로 마주나는데, 줄기와 잎에 길게 퍼진 털이 빽빽하게 나는 특징이 있다. 7~8월에 꽃을 피우고 9~10월에 씨를 맺는다. 서식조건이 적합하고 안정된 곳에서는 씨앗으로 퍼지지만 땅속줄기로도 번져나가기도 한다.
국립생태원 멸종위기종복원센터는 지난해 8월 청송군 주방천 일대에 큰바늘꽃 200개체를 이식했다. 1년이 지난 지금 자연 번식으로 개체수가 2.5배 증가해 현재는 500여 개체가 생육하고 있는 것으로 확인됐다.
대부분의 개체는 건강하게 연보랏빛 꽃을 피웠고, 그 주변으로 재래꿀벌, 배추흰나비 등 곤충들이 날아들었다. 일부 개체가 뿌리줄기를 뻗어 이식지 보호 울타리 밖으로 번져나가는 모습도 관찰됐다.
이번 이식지는 과거에 큰바늘꽃이 자생했으나 인위적인 개발로 야생 개체군이 사라진 지역이다. 큰바늘꽃의 성공적인 현지 적응은 과거 서식지에서 사라진 야생생물이 우리의 복원 노력을 통해 자연에 다시 정착할 수 있다는 가능성을 보여준다.
국립생태원 멸종위기종복원센터는 큰바늘꽃을 비롯한 다양한 멸종위기종의 복원 연구와 교육을 진행하고 있다. 이를 통해 멸종위기종의 개체군 회복과 생물다양성 증진을 도모하고, 생태계 건강성 회복에 대한 국민공감대 형성을 위해 노력하고 있다.
국립생태원 강재신 멸종위기종복원센터장은 “큰바늘꽃의 현지 적응 기술 개발은 한반도의 생물다양성을 지키는 든든한 디딤돌이 될 것”이라며, “앞으로도 묵묵히 멸종위기종을 복원해 자연과 인간이 조화롭게 공존할 수 있는 기반을 넓혀가겠다”고 말했다.

title: Reactivation of the Qardabiya-Sadada section Man-Made River system after a 13-year hiatus
content:
The National Development Agency (NDA) and the Man-Made River Authority held a ceremony yesterday in the city of Sirte to mark the reactivation of the Qardabiya-Sadada section of the Man-Made River system. This milestone follows the completion of rehabilitation works overseen by the NDA—after the system had been out of service for over 13 years—to restore it to full operational status.
The rehabilitation process involved the procurement and installation of more than 250 valves to replace missing or damaged ones. These efforts spanned nearly a year and were followed by the refilling and operational testing of the system to ensure it was fully ready for service.
The ceremony featured the opening of the water inlet valve for the first phase, allowing it to connect with the water from the second phase. This integration enhances the synergy between the two systems and provides greater flexibility in water supply, particularly during maintenance and emergency situations.
The reactivation of the system, the NDA said, represents a significant step toward bolstering water security and protecting vital infrastructure; it stands as a tangible manifestation of the ongoing drive for construction, development, and public service.

title: Nachwuchsrekord bei Weißstörchen
content:
Mit 46 Brutpaaren wurde außerdem der Rekord von 1994 eingestellt, während bei den Jungvögeln pro Paar mit durchschnittlich rund drei Küken ein Allzeit-Hoch erzielt wurde. Grundlage ist ein Monitoring des Vereins „AURING“ im WWF-Auenreservat, auf dem Schlossgelände, in Markthof und in der Stadt Marchegg.
„Die erfreulichen Zahlen sind ein großer Erfolg für den Artenschutz und verdeutlichen die Bedeutung des WWF-Auenreservats für die Biodiversität“, sagte Jurrien Westerhof vom WWF.
Ideale Bedingungen für Bruterfolg
Weißstörche brauchen geeignete Brutplätze und nahrungsreiche Flächen in ihrer unmittelbaren Umgebung. „In Marchegg kommt beides zusammen, das macht dieses Gebiet so wertvoll für ihren Bruterfolg“, erklärte Karin Donnerbaum, Biologin beim Verein „AURING“. Zur Qualität des Lebensraums trage auch die naturnahe Bewirtschaftung des Reservats bei, hieß es.
„Die Beweidung durch eine Rinderherde und unsere halbwilden Konik-Pferde schafft wertvolle Strukturen, wie zum Beispiel Dunghaufen, Suhlen und unterschiedliche Vegetationsstufen. Davon profitieren neben den Weißstörchen noch viele weitere Tier- und Pflanzenarten“, sagte Westerhof – mehr dazu in Beweidete Auwiesen als wirksame CO2-Speicher (noe.ORF.at; 7.9.2025).
Das rund 1.100 Hektar große Auenreservat Marchegg beherbergt mehr als 500 gefährdete Tier- und Pflanzenarten – neben Weißstörchen etwa auch Seeadler, Schwarzstörche und Rotmilane. „Marchegg zeigt, was langfristiger Naturschutz bewirken kann“, so der WWF, der von der Politik erneut eine österreichweite Renaturierungsoffensive fordert.

title: Agency says sea turtle eggs laid on California beaches are a first for the US West Coast
content:
A reptile believed to be struggling in sand at a Southern California beach was simply making history: a sea turtle laying eggs on the U.S. West Coast.
And three days later, there were more. An olive ridley turtle—maybe the same one—laid eggs on Sept. 19, a few miles away near the Huntington Beach Pier in Orange County, authorities said.
"This is the first-ever recorded natural nesting for any sea turtle species" on the West Coast, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's West Coast Fisheries division said on Facebook.
Olive ridley turtles are the smallest of sea turtles, with adults weighing up to 100 pounds (45.3 kilograms). NOAA said they're found worldwide but primarily in the tropical waters of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans.
The first nesting spot was near Seal Beach on Sept. 16, followed by the discovery at Huntington Beach. Both sites were subsequently fenced off. Incubation typically lasts 45 to 60 days, NOAA said.
"We're excited about it," said Trevor McDonald, marine safety chief at the Huntington Beach Fire Department.
Lifeguards patrolling at night saw a turtle digging in the sand and thought "maybe this turtle is sick. We just don't see this very often," McDonald said. "Then they observed the turtle starting to lay eggs."
Heidi Stephen said her 9-year-old son, Jude, begged her to take him to Huntington Beach to see the nest Tuesday.
"It's so magical," Stephen said.
George Zamora said he hopes the eggs can survive any impact from tides, storms and popular beach events.
"Let them do their thing," Zamora said. "Let them be born."

title: El Salvador: las mujeres que se protegen de inundaciones y sequías con ciencia comunitaria
content:
- Un grupo de 19 personas, en su mayoría mujeres, se adaptan al cambio climático en el municipio de Ahuachapán Sur, una zona golpeada por sequías y lluvias extremas.
- Son 13 comunidades las que operan un sistema de prevención y mitigación de riesgo que se comunica vía Whatsapp.
- La red de monitoras tiene 13 puntos de monitoreo de lluvia, cuatro de temperatura y humedad y 11 puntos de muestreo físico químico de agua en los manglares del municipio, lo que les permite salvar vidas y proteger sus ecosistemas.
- Con apoyo de varias instituciones, las mujeres han creado un banco de semillas criollas resistentes al clima extremo que incluye plantas como maíz negro y amarillo, tomate, pepino, chile jalapeño, berenjena, pipianes y flor de Jamaica.
La temporada de huracanes 2026 en el Pacífico y las alertas internacionales por los impactos severos asociados con el fenómeno de El Niño, activaron a un grupo de mujeres en la ruralidad del municipio de Ahuachapán Sur, en la costa occidental de El Salvador. Estas mujeres intentan conservar los manglares del Sitio Ramsar Complejo Barra de Santiago, para proteger a las comunidades que padecen los daños y pérdidas que deja el cambio climático en el país.
Con frecuencia ellas se reúnen para intercambiar semillas criollas resistentes al clima extremo, vender productos agroecológicos y hablar de lo que aprenden en la Red de Monitoreo Hidroclimático Comunitario. Esta red surgió de forma espontánea en 1998, tras los impactos del huracán Mitch en las comunidades costeras del departamento de Ahuachapán y, poco a poco, se fue tecnificando con la llegada de varias ONG. Actualmente, el grupo está conformado por 19 personas: 12 mujeres y siete hombres que trabajan en la adaptación climática.
Las mujeres, que se han enfrentado a tormentas tropicales, huracanes y sequías, se han convertido en monitoras del clima mientras generan datos científicos con apoyo técnico de la organización no gubernamental Unidad Ecológica Salvadoreña (UNES) y la Universidad de El Salvador (UES). Como resultado del monitoreo de lluvias, emiten alertas tempranas para evitar muertes por desbordamientos de ríos e inundaciones, y hasta para ajustar los tiempos de sus cultivos si se pronostican sequías prolongadas.
A finales de abril de 2026, las monitoras se reunieron en los manglares del cantón Garita Palmera, que forma parte del Complejo Barra de Santiago. Este ecosistema está afectado por la salinización del agua y la erosión costera causada por actividades agrícolas que hacen uso desmedido del agua de los ríos, pero también por el impacto de tormentas tropicales y el incremento en la frecuencia del mar de fondo, un fenómeno natural que incrementa el oleaje del océano Pacífico.
Este escenario no es desconocido para las mujeres más veteranas de la red, que en aquella reunión de abril entrenaron a una docena de nuevas integrantes, con la esperanza de ampliar la cobertura del monitoreo hidroclimático.
Con pluviómetro en mano, Glenda Lara Mangandi explica que su trabajo es hacer el seguimiento a la lluvia acumulada durante las últimas 24 horas. Los resultados se registran en la bitácora de lluvias y se comparten en grupos de WhatsApp. “Esto nos sirve para alertar a todos los grupos”, afirma Lara.
Bajo este esquema de gestión de riesgo operan 13 comunidades que monitorean la lluvia en la cuenca alta, media y baja de los ríos Paz y Cara Sucia – San Pedro Belén, en los distritos de San Francisco Menéndez, Jujutla y Guaymango, del municipio de Ahuachapán Sur, en el departamento de Ahuachapán. La gestión de riesgo llega hasta Metalío, una playa del distrito de Acajutla, en el municipio de Sonsonate Oeste, en donde desemboca el río Cauta que nace en Ahuachapán.
Con el paso cada vez más frecuente de eventos naturales potenciados por el cambio climático y con la práctica constante en el uso de dispositivos para medir el clima, estas mujeres han entendido que la ciencia y la tecnología son sus mejores herramientas para evitar desastres en las comunidades rurales en las que viven.
Comunidades que se blindan con ciencia
El huracán Mitch dejó grandes retos, explica Sara García, una reconocida defensora ambiental del occidente salvadoreño e integrante de la red de monitoras desde sus inicios. Mitch está entre los 10 huracanes más intensos del Atlántico registrados por la Oficina Nacional de Administración Oceánica y Atmosférica (NOAA, por sus siglas en inglés), y uno de los más letales, dejando a su paso 11 000 muertes, 8000 desaparecidos y daños por 5000 millones de dólares en 1998.
El impacto fue severo en la costa salvadoreña. Por eso, cuenta García, el mayor reto de las comunidades del municipio de Ahuachapán Sur fue trabajar en la mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático, a tal punto que el tema se convirtió en un eje principal de la organización comunitaria.
A casi 28 años del huracán Mitch, las comunidades tienen 13 puntos de monitoreo de lluvia, cuatro de temperatura y humedad, y once puntos de muestreo físico químico de agua en los manglares del municipio, ecosistemas que sirven como barrera natural contra inundaciones, erosión costera y mareas altas.
Cada evento climático les deja más experiencia, pero García no niega que uno de los que más le marcó fue el paso de la tormenta tropical Julia en octubre de 2022. En ese momento monitoreaba Guaymango, en Ahuachapán Sur, por donde corre el agua que alimenta las subcuencas de los ríos Cauta, Metalío y Chalata que desembocan en el departamento de Sonsonate. “Nosotros medimos la intensidad de la lluvia. Y teníamos ya más de seis horas de lluvias intensas”, narra.
García emitió la alerta temprana hacia la red de monitoras de la cuenca baja, en las playas Metalillo, Monzón y Costa Azul, en Sonsonate, y ellas se comunicaron directamente con un centro de salud cercano que se encargó de evacuar a cuatro personas en zonas vulnerables de la desembocadura de los tres ríos.
Dos horas después de la alerta, “el río se desbordó totalmente y se metió a todas esas casas a más de un metro de altura», cuenta la monitora de Guaymango. A pesar del impacto en términos materiales, el monitoreo logró uno de sus objetivos supremos: salvar vidas.
Adaptación climática comunitaria
En tiempos de crisis climática, y ante la falta de un sistema de protección civil integral y eficiente, el dato científico comunitario cobra importancia. “Generar estos avisos oportunos desde las comunidades que componen el sistema de monitoreo, ayuda a reducir los impactos en pérdidas y daños que se puedan ocasionar debido a estos eventos extremos”, reconoce Asunción Martínez, encargada del proyecto de monitoreo climático en la UNES.
La adaptación climática de la Red de Monitoreo Hidroclimático Comunitario no sólo incorpora un sistema de gestión de riesgos que se comunica vía WhatsApp, sino que han creado un banco de semillas criollas resistentes al clima costero, impulsan jornadas para limpiar y remover los sedimentos que obstruyen los canales del manglar y trabajan en la reforestación del Complejo Barra de Santiago.
En la reunión que las mujeres tuvieron en Garita Palmera, Ana de Jesús González, agricultora de la tercera edad que participa como monitora climática, explicó a Mongabay Latam que para proteger sus cultivos de las posibles inundaciones, los saca de la tierra y los traslada a estantes. El Porvenir, la zona rural donde ella vive, se inunda con el desborde del río El Chino. “Nos toca andar embotadas porque se nos mete el agua”, describe.
Cuando eso pasa, lo primero que las mujeres pierden son sus cultivos: “Las plantitas se nos mueren”, repite González. Y ese es un lujo que ellas no se pueden permitir, ya que la venta de frutas y vegetales agroecológicos en ferias locales es su modo de subsistencia en la ruralidad de uno de los sitios más pobres de El Salvador.
De hecho, en 2024 el Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD) en El Salvador hizo un análisis socioeconómico donde resalta que el 50 % de la población en el municipio de Ahuachapán Sur se encuentra en condición de pobreza multidimensional; es decir, que vive con menores oportunidades para acceder a salud, educación y calidad de vida. Por eso la soberanía alimentaria es vital para la subsistencia de estas comunidades.
Glenda Lara Mangandi reconoce la importancia de estar informadas. “Antes no sabíamos que al haber mucha lluvia se perdían las hortalizas”, destaca la monitora de El Porvenir. Ahora, el sistema de monitoreo hidroclimático les permite generar datos y comunicarlos oportunamente a las personas que se dedican a la agricultura. “Se les informa cuando habrá mucha o poca lluvia y cuando habrá resequedad”, recalca.
Los desafíos que impone El Niño
Uno de los retos inminentes para las mujeres monitoras es el actual fenómeno de El Niño. El 4 de agosto, la Organización Meteorológica Mundial (OMM) y la Organización Panamericana de la Salud (OPS) advirtieron que existen las condiciones para que El Niño “evolucione de un evento fuerte a muy fuerte”. Bárbara Tapia, de la OMM, dijo dos días después que el máximo punto de El Niño será perceptible entre noviembre de 2026 y enero de 2027, por lo que la organización recomienda la “articulación de autoridades nacionales, subnacionales y locales”, aseguró Tapia.
La NOAA estima un 69 % de probabilidades para que, entre octubre y noviembre de 2026, el fenómeno “se convierta en un evento histórico que superaría la intensidad de los eventos de El Niño previos en el registro que data desde 1950”, detalla en un comunicado del 13 de agosto.
Desde el 23 de junio, el Ministerio de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (MARN) ya alertaba sobre el inicio temprano de la canícula —evento climático que ocurre durante el verano y se caracteriza por una disminución o ausencia de lluvias acompañada de un aumento significativo de las temperaturas—. La alerta máxima se dio el 25 de agosto, cuando la dirección general de Protección Civil de El Salvador declaró alerta roja a nivel nacional por sequía.
Sin embargo, esto no tomó por sorpresa a la Red de Monitoreo Hidroclimático Comunitario. Antes de las advertencias meteorológicas, entre marzo y abril, las monitoras de Ahuachapán Sur ya registraban datos de lluvia escasa asociados con El Niño. “En las comunidades de Paz y Progreso cayeron 14.4 mililitros (ml) de lluvia; en Bola de Monte, 4.0 ml, que es poquito; en El Tamarindo 1.4 ml”, detalla Lara Mangandi al acceder al registro del 26 de abril que realizó el grupo de mujeres en Garita Palmera.
A la alerta por el aumento de las temperaturas en El Salvador se suma la alarma por riesgos en salud. En un informe elaborado por la Organización Panamericana de la Salud (OPS), la entidad alertó que entre los principales riesgos se encuentran el cólera y otras enfermedades transmitidas por el agua, así como enfermedades transmitidas por vectores, como la malaria, el dengue, el zika y el chikunguña.
Es por eso que las monitoras de Guaymango ya preparaban repelentes naturales para combatir las plagas que proliferan con el calor. Sara García tiene claro que hay una variedad de insectos que afectan directamente sus cultivos agroecológicos, “como la cochinilla, la mosca amarilla, el gusano foliar”. Los repelentes son a base de leche solo para ahuyentar a los animales, “no los podemos matar”, recalca.
El modelo de resiliencia de la Red de Monitoreo Hidroclimático Comunitario ha logrado avances significativos, pero también debe enfrentar retos que persisten. Asunción Martínez, de la UNES, explica que el mayor problema para las comunidades del municipio de Ahuachapán Sur es que la crisis climática no les da tiempo de recuperarse de los daños y pérdidas de un evento, pues inmediatamente llega uno nuevo. “No terminamos de recuperarnos de un evento extremo, como sequía o precipitaciones, cuando ya viene otra situación que desencadena otras problemáticas”, explica.
El Salvador tiene un escenario crítico con los impactos previstos de El Niño en Centroamérica: déficit de precipitaciones, sequías prolongadas y aumento de la temperatura. “Estas condiciones afectarán directamente los medios de vida de la población y entre estos la agricultura de subsistencia, principal medio de vida de millones de familias rurales», alerta la UNES.
Como parte de la adaptación climática, esta organización acompaña la producción agroecológica que emprenden estas monitoras climáticas, a través de su santuario de semillas criollas resistentes al calor de la costa.
La misma encargada de la estación pluviométrica de El Porvenir, Glenda Lara Mangandi, es la guardiana de este banco que, entre otras semillas, conserva maíz negro y amarillo, tomate, chile jalapeño, berenjena, pipianes y flor de Jamaica. Las comunidades también han diversificado estos cultivos con otros como la yuca, el plátano, el rábano y el pepino.
Guardianas del manglar
Las comunidades costeras del departamento de Ahuachapán han puesto en práctica la adaptación climática para estar mejor preparadas ante los desastres y garantizar su seguridad alimentaria. Pero no sólo esto, también se han embarrado el cuerpo de lodo para restaurar el Sitio Ramsar y Área Natural Protegida Complejo Barra de Santiago, donde los manglares están muriendo debido al bloqueo de varios canales, lo que impide el flujo natural del agua dulce y salada que mantiene la salud del ecosistema.
Las mujeres monitoras han pasado a la acción y realizan limpieza de los canales para que el agua salobre fluya y el ecosistema se restaure naturalmente; mientras que, por otro lado, reforestan con mangle negro (Avicennia germinans) o istatén, como se le conoce a este árbol en El Salvador. Aseguran que sólo en 2023, junto con la UNES, reforestaron 1.5 hectáreas en la zona aledaña al canal Los Tubos, en Garita Palmera. Para ellas, se trata de un gran logro pues, aunque la cifra parezca pequeña, es toda una hazaña que la mayoría del manglar en esa área aún sobreviva en 2026.
Durante los últimos 35 años, Néstor Herrera, biólogo independiente, ha dado seguimiento a la evolución del Complejo Barra de Santiago y asegura que, desde 1991, el ecosistema ya reflejaba los daños por el azolvamiento de canales y la salinización del agua. Según Herrera, en la zona alta de la cuenca la agricultura industrial —sobre todo de caña— desvía los ríos para sus cultivos, diezmando la cantidad de agua dulce que recibe el manglar.
Cuando los canales se reducen, explica el biólogo, los habitantes ya no pueden navegar y no hay pesca. “Hay pérdida de bancos de conchas, cangrejos, y toda la proteína que alimenta a las comunidades”, dice.
Herrera reconoce que sin el trabajo comunitario este manglar estaría en peores condiciones, pero teme que los esfuerzos comunitarios se queden cortos ante la crisis que se vive. “Estamos teniendo un invierno muy seco, muy bajo en agua, entonces no importa si han desasolvado los canales [el proceso que consiste en remover los sedimentos acumulados en los canales para permitir que el agua fluya] porque no va a haber agua”.
Por años, las comunidades han pedido a diferentes gobiernos que dejen maquinaria permanente para la liberación rápida de las bocanas que cada vez se bloquean con más frecuencia debido a la ocurrencia de fenómenos como el mar de fondo —evento de oleaje alto que suele agravarse cuando hay sistemas ciclónicos cerca de la región—. Sin embargo, el apoyo llega esporádicamente.
Para evaluar el estado de los ecosistemas, su biodiversidad y la efectividad de la reforestación, Asunción Martínez de la UNES comenta que las guardianas del manglar hacen constantes monitoreos de los parámetros biofísicos del agua con apoyo de la Universidad de El Salvador (UES). Tener el dato científico les sirve como respaldo para exigir la protección de su territorio.
Esa apropiación comunitaria de la información científica ha representado una esperanza para la gente que vive en la costa de Ahuachapán. Sienten que ya tienen mejores herramientas para responder a los efectos de los fenómenos naturales potenciados por el cambio climático y cada vez son más conscientes de lo importante que es recuperar el manglar del Complejo Barra de Santiago, su escudo protector para los embates de la naturaleza.
*Este reportaje es una alianza periodística entre Mongabay Latam y Mala Yerba de El Salvador.

title: How Influencer Bittu Tabahi Mobilized Delhi Youth To Clean Up The Yamuna River
content:
Bittu Tabahi again came forward to champion environmental restoration, bringing his hands-on cleanliness campaign to the National Capital Region to restore the polluted banks of the Yamuna River. For decades, urban neglect, untreated industrial effluents, domestic sewage, and solid waste dumping have turned stretches of this majestic river into one of the most polluted waterways in the world. During festival seasons, thick layers of toxic chemical foam float across its surface, presenting a heartbreaking visual of environmental degradation.
While many express anger online or lament the situation from afar, popular digital creator Bittu Tabahi chose a different path. Recognizing that online complaints alone would not clear the sludge, he stepped directly onto the riverbanks to take hands-on action, inspiring a new wave of youth environmental activism in Delhi.
From Screen to Shoreline: Taking Direct Action
Known for his engaging online presence and relatable content, Bittu felt a growing responsibility toward his surrounding community. Seeing the Yamuna choked under mountains of single-use plastic, rotting ceremonial offerings, and synthetic clothing, he decided that waiting for external cleanup drives was no longer an option.
Equipped with basic boots, gloves, and garbage bags, Bittu began visiting polluted stretches along the river. Wading knee-deep into murky, odorous waters, he started pulling out submerged plastic waste item by item. Cleaning a polluted river manually is physically taxing and hazardous. The toxic water poses constant risks of waterborne infections, skin rashes, and respiratory discomfort from noxious fumes. Undeterred by these health risks, Bittu maintained a steady cleanup schedule, turning a solitary initiative into a persistent campaign for environmental dignity.
Turning Social Media Clout into Ground-Level Action
What sets Bittu’s effort apart is his strategic use of digital storytelling. Instead of publishing polished, artificial videos, he shared raw, unedited footage of his daily cleanup drives on his social media channels. His videos highlighted the harsh reality of urban waste while showing the immediate physical relief brought by clearing garbage from the shoreline.
His authentic videos quickly caught the attention of young viewers across Delhi and surrounding regions. Bittu utilized his platform not just for entertainment, but as a rallying cry for Gen Z. He invited his followers, students, and local residents to join him on weekends, transforming social media scroll time into active community service.
Within weeks, dozens of enthusiastic volunteers began arriving at the riverbanks. Armed with gloves and trash pickers, groups of young citizens worked side by side, pulling quintals of plastic waste out of the river and piling it systematically for municipal disposal.
Addressing the Root Cause of River Pollution
Bittu understands that physically removing garbage from a river is only half the battle; stopping waste at its source is equally critical. Through his videos and on-ground interactions, he continuously educates the public on responsible waste management. He appeals directly to citizens to stop throwing plastic bags, floral decorations in synthetic wrapping, and household debris into open drains and river channels.
By bridging entertainment, youth culture, and civic duty, Bittu Tabahi is proving that social media influencers can serve as powerful catalysts for environmental accountability. His work challenges the stereotype that online creators are detached from real-world issues, showing that digital popularity can be channeled into meaningful environmental stewardship.
Building a Lasting Legacy for Urban Rivers
The Yamuna cleanup movement led by Bittu Tabahi demonstrates the incredible potential of youth-led grassroots action. By demonstrating that one determined individual can inspire hundreds to clean up their own city, he offers a scalable blueprint for urban ecological restoration across India.
His journey serves as a powerful reminder that saving our natural heritage does not always require complex technology or massive budgets. It simply requires courage, physical commitment, and a refusal to remain silent while our rivers choke under human neglect.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Bittu Tabahi’s relentless effort to clean the Yamuna exemplifies the transformative potential of youth leadership in India. In an era where social media is frequently criticized for promoting superficial trends, his ground-level action demonstrates how digital reach can be harnessed to solve critical environmental crises.
His work highlights a vital shift among young Indians who demand action over debate. As urban water bodies face unprecedented pollution, community-led initiatives like Bittu’s demonstrate that citizens hold the power to revitalize our natural ecosystems. Protecting our rivers is not merely an administrative task; it is a shared civic responsibility that defines the future of our nation.
How can municipal corporations in major Indian cities collaborate with digital creators and youth volunteers to sustain community-led river cleanup drives?

title: ¿Pueden las baterías usadas del coche eléctrico tener una segunda vida como almacenamiento de renovables? Asturias dice sí
content: Una batería puede haber dejado de ser lo bastante buena para un coche eléctrico y, sin embargo, todavía tener mucha vida por delante. El informe de la Fundación Asturiana de la Energía (FAEN) Recuperación de materiales estratégicos de las baterías dentro del sector Automovilístico: Modelos de economía circular y su implementación en Asturias plantea una posibilidad muy interesante: dar una segunda vida a las baterías convirtiéndolas en sistemas estacionarios de almacenamiento de energía. Y mejor si esa energía procede de fuentes renovables. Un mercado al alza. Según datos del último Global EV Outlook 2026 de la Agencia Internacional de la Energía (AIE), este 2026 se van a vender 23 millones de vehículos eléctricos. Una cifra que hace apenas unos años costaba imaginar, pero que hoy, con los bandazos de los precios de los combustibles y una mayor conciencia medioambiental, parece más natural que nunca. Esto va a conllevar, según el mismo documento, un crecimiento de la producción de baterías de hasta cuatro veces de aquí a 2030, y, por tanto también una intensa competencia por asegurarse el acceso a minerales críticos como el litio, el cobalto y el níquel. Sin embargo, el acceso a estos componentes se está volviendo cada vez más complejo, a múltiples niveles, desde el operativo al geopolítico. De ahí que resulte crucial optimizar todo el ciclo operativo de las baterías y evitar su descarte prematuro. En Xataka Esto que parece un edificio a medio construir en China es una batería gigante que funciona con gravedad Buscando una segunda oportunidad. Como explica el informe de FAEN, se suele asumir que la batería de un vehículo eléctrico llega al final de su vida cuando su capacidad desciende al 70% de la que tenía de fábrica. Aunque para la movilidad esa pérdida de autonomía significa que la batería ha dejado de ser funcional y que hay que reemplazarla, lo cierto es que sigue siendo una muy buena marca para otro tipo de aplicaciones. Es el caso de los sistemas estacionarios de almacenamiento de energía que podrían usarse tanto en contextos residenciales como industriales. Según el informe, estas baterías, aunque ya no sean útiles para el coche eléctrico, pueden seguir almacenando cantidades nada desdeñables de energía que puedan usarse en otras situaciones, como para hacer frente a picos de demanda industrial, complementar instalaciones renovables, o, incluso, alimentar la carga de vehículos eléctricos con baterías aptas. Las renovables, perfect match. Asturias ya genera electricidad renovable. En mayo de 2026, el estudio cuenta 24 parques eólicos que Asturias tiene en funcionamiento, con una potencia instalada de 698,66 MW. Lo que plantea el estudio es que esta segunda vida encajaría a la perfección con el despliegue de las energías renovables en el principado. El problema es que producir electricidad cuando sopla el viento o brilla el sol en el cielo no significa necesariamente producirla cuando alguien la necesita. De ahí que las baterías de segunda vida puedan actuar como una pieza más de esa apuesta asturiana por las renovables y almacenar la energía cuando sobra para utilizarla cuando hace falta. Asturias tiene una ventana de oportunidad. Y España también. La sostenibilidad no es el único argumento. El informe recoge estudios según los cuales el uso de baterías de segunda vida podría reducir el coste nivelado de la energía en determinadas aplicaciones, con descensos que en algunos casos llegan hasta el 57%. De acuerdo con FAEN, esto supondría abrir la puerta a nuevos modelos de actividad económica en una cadena industrial que aún está desarrollándose y que podría cobrar una relevancia mundial. Y no solo con las baterías que valen: también con las que ya no son adecuadas para una segunda vida. No todas las baterías tendrán una segunda vida. El estudio contempla la posibilidad de que algunas de esas baterías ya estarán demasiado degradadas o dañadas, mientras que otras, simplemente, no resultarán rentables de reutilizar. En ese caso, ahí entrarán en juego tecnologías como la hidrometalurgia, la pirometalurgia y la biometalurgia, tres de las vías que analiza el estudio de FAEN para recuperar los preciados materiales de los que se componen las baterías.
